nodes.name: Courcelle's theorem
nodes.statement: In particular, for graphs of bounded treewidth, Courcelle's theorem states that any property that is definable in the logic \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace with modulo counting predicate, denoted \CMSO, can be recognized by a tree automaton \cite{TMSOLOG1}.
assumptions: for graphs of bounded treewidth
conclusions: any property that is definable in the logic \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace with modulo counting predicate, denoted \CMSO, can be recognized by a tree automaton

nodes.name: Bojanczyk-Pilipczuk theorem (converse of Courcelle's theorem)
nodes.statement:
The converse statement -- whether recognisability by a tree automaton implies definability in \CMSO\ on graphs of bounded treewidth --
was conjectured by Courcelle in \cite{TMSOLOG1} and finally settled by Boja\'nczyk and Pilipczuk \cite{BojanczykP16}.
nodes.statement_short: On graphs of bounded treewidth, recognisability by a tree automaton implies CMSO-definability (conjectured by Courcelle).

nodes.name: MSO-transducing clique-width decompositions of bounded linear clique-width graphs
nodes.statement:
It is known that clique-width decompositions can be \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-transduced for
graphs of bounded linear clique-width \cite{BojanczykGP21}.
assumptions: graphs of bounded linear clique-width
conclusions: clique-width decompositions can be \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-transduced

nodes.name: MSO-transducing clique-width decompositions in general
nodes.statement:
However, it is unknown if clique-width decompositions can be \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-transduced in general. In fact,
this question remained open even for distance-hereditary graphs, which are precisely graphs of rank-width 1 (thus, of constant clique-width).

nodes.name: Removing the order from Courcelle's order-invariant MSO transductions
nodes.statement:
It was left as an open question whether one can get rid of the order (see for instance
\cite{CourcelleT12} where an overview of the result on hierarchical decompositions was given).

nodes.name: Summary of CMSO-transductions of tree-like decompositions
nodes.statement_short: Non-deterministic CMSO[2]-transductions output laminar trees, modular/split/bi-join decompositions, cotrees, and weakly-(bi)partitive trees.
conclusions: There are non-deterministic \CMSO[2]-transductions $\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_7$ such that:
nodes.label: thm:summary

nodes.name: CMSO-transduction of width-1 rank-decompositions of rank-width-1 graphs
nodes.statement:
It is worth mentionning that a corollary of
\autoref{thm:summary}(4) is a \CMSO-transduction outputting a rank-decomposition of width $1$ for every graph of rank-width $1$.
assumptions: for every graph of rank-width $1$
conclusions: a \CMSO-transduction outputting a rank-decomposition of width $1$

nodes.name: Vertex and edge sets of a graph
Edge notation uv
nodes.statement: We denote by \defd{uv} an edge~$(u,v)\in E(G)$.

nodes.name: Undirected graph
nodes.statement:
An undirected graph is no more than a directed graph
for which~$E(G)$ is symmetric ({\em i.e.}, $uv\in E(G)\iff vu\in E(G)$).

nodes.name: Induced subgraph G[Z]
nodes.statement:
Given a subset~$Z$ of~$V(G)$,
we denote by \defd{$G[Z]$} the sub-graph of~$G$ induced by~$Z$.

nodes.name: Tree
nodes.statement: A \defd{tree} is a connected undirected graph without cycles.

nodes.name: Nodes, leaves and inner nodes of a tree
nodes.statement:
In particular, vertices are called~\defd{nodes},
nodes of degree at most~$1$ are called \defd{leaves},
and nodes of degree greater than~$1$ are called \defd{inner}.

nodes.name: Leaf set L(T)
nodes.statement:
The set of leaves is denoted~\defd{$L(T)$};
thus the set of inner nodes is~$V(T)\setminus L(T)$.

nodes.name: Component T^t_s
nodes.statement: For a node $t$ of a tree $T$ and a neighbor $s$ of $t$, we denote by $T^t_s$ the connected component of $T-t$ containing $s$.

nodes.name: Rooted tree and root
nodes.statement:
We sometimes consider \defd{rooted trees},
namely trees with a distinguished node, called the \defd{root}.

nodes.name: Parent, child, sibling, ancestor, descendant
nodes.statement:
Rooted trees enjoy a natural orientation of their edges
toward the root,
which induces the usual notions of
\defd{parent}, \defd{child}, \defd{sibling}, \defd{ancestor} and \defd{descendant}.

nodes.name: Proper ancestors and descendants
nodes.statement:
We refer to ancestors (resp.\xspace descendants) of a node
that are not the node itself
as \defd{proper ancestors} (resp.\xspace \defd{proper descendants}).

nodes.name: Subtree T_t
nodes.statement:
For a node~$t$ of a rooted tree~$T$,
we denote by~\defd{$T_t$} the subtree of~$T$ rooted in~$t$
({\em i.e.}, the restriction of~$T$ to the set of descendants of~$t$).

nodes.name: Set system
nodes.statement:
A \defd{set system} is a pair~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
where~$U$ is a finite set, called the \defd{universe},
and~$\mathcal{S}$ is a family of subsets of~$U$
where~$\emptyset\notin\mathcal{S}$,
$U\in\mathcal{S}$,
and~$\{a\}\in\mathcal{S}$ for every~$a\in U$.
nodes.statement_short: A finite universe with a family of subsets containing U and all singletons but not the empty set.

nodes.name: Overlapping sets
nodes.statement:
Two sets~$X$ and~$Y$ \defd{overlap}
if they are neither disjoint nor related by containment.

nodes.name: Laminar set system
nodes.statement:
A set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
is said to be \defd{laminar} (aka\xspace \emph{overlap-free})
when no two sets from~$\mathcal{S}$ overlap.

nodes.name: Laminar set family
Laminar tree of a set system
nodes.statement:
A laminar family~$\mathcal{S}$ of subsets of~$U$
naturally defines a rooted tree
where the nodes are the sets from~$\mathcal{S}$,
the root is~$U$,
and the ancestor relation corresponds to set inclusion.
We call this rooted tree
the \defd{laminar tree of~$U$ induced by $\mathcal{S}$}
(or \defd{laminar tree of~$(U,\mathcal{S})$}).\xspace
In this rooted tree,
the leaves are the singletons~$\{x\}$ for~$x\in U$,
which we identify with the elements themselves.
That is to say, $L(T)=U$.
nodes.statement_short: The rooted tree whose nodes are the sets of a laminar family, ordered by inclusion, with root U and singleton leaves.

nodes.name: Inner nodes of laminar trees have at least two children
nodes.statement:
Laminar trees have the property
that each inner node has at least two children.
conclusions: each inner node has at least two children

nodes.name: Extended vocabulary
nodes.statement:
Define an \defd{(extended) vocabulary} to be a set of symbols,
each being either a \emph{relation} name~$R$ with associated arity~\defd{$\operatorname{ar}(R)\in\mathbb{N}$},
or a \emph{set predicate} name~$P$ with associated arity~\defd{$\operatorname{ar}(P)\in\mathbb{N}$}.
differentia:
each being either a \emph{relation} name~$R$ with associated arity~\defd{$\operatorname{ar}(R)\in\mathbb{N}$},
    or a \emph{set predicate} name~$P$ with associated arity~\defd{$\operatorname{ar}(P)\in\mathbb{N}$}

nodes.name: Relational vocabulary
nodes.statement: A \defd{relational vocabulary} is an extended vocabulary in which every symbol is a relation name.
differentia: every symbol is a relation name

nodes.name: Extended relational structure (Sigma-structure)
nodes.statement:
Let~$\Sigma$ be a vocabulary.
An \defd{extended relational structure over~$\Sigma$} (\defd{$\Sigma$-structure})
is a structure $\mathbb{A}=\langle U_{\mathbb{A}}, (Q_{\mathbb{A}})_{Q\in \Sigma}\rangle$
consisting on the one hand of a set~\defd{$U_\mathbb{A}$} called \defd{universe},
and on the other hand, for each symbol~$Q$ in~$\Sigma$,
an \defd{interpretation~$Q_{\mathbb{A}}$ of~$Q$},
which is a relation of arity~$\operatorname{ar}(Q)$
either over the universe if~$Q$ is a relation name,
or over the family of subsets of the universe if~$Q$ is a set predicate name.
nodes.statement_short: A universe together with an interpretation of each relation name over elements and each set predicate over subsets.

nodes.name: Relational structure
nodes.statement: When~$\Sigma$ is not extended, $\mathbb{A}$ is simply a \defd{relational structure}.

nodes.name: Structure inclusion relation
nodes.statement_short: A is included in B when B's vocabulary and universe extend A's and every symbol of A is interpreted identically.

nodes.name: Union of structures
nodes.statement:
We write~\defd{$\mathbb{A}\sqcup\mathbb{B}$}
to denote the $(\Sigma\cup\Gamma)$-structure
consisting of the universe~$U_{\mathbb{A}}\cup U_{\mathbb{B}}$
and, for each symbol~$Q\in\Sigma\cup\Gamma$,
the interpretation $Q_{\mathbb{A}\sqcup\mathbb{B}}$
which is~$Q_{\mathbb{A}}$, $Q_{\mathbb{B}}$, or~$Q_{\mathbb{A}}\cup Q_{\mathbb{B}}$
according to whether~$Q$ belongs to~$\Sigma\setminus\Gamma$, to~$\Gamma\setminus\Sigma$, or to~$\Sigma\cap\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: The union structure over the union vocabulary and universes, taking unions of interpretations of shared symbols.

nodes.name: Monadic second order logic (MSO)
nodes.statement:
To describe properties of (extended) relational structures, we use \defd{monadic second order logic} (\defd{\ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace}) and refer for instance to
\cite{CE09,FunkMN22,Hlineny06,Strozecki11} for the definition of \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace on extended relational structures such as matroids or set systems in general. This logic allows quantification both over single elements of the universe
and over subsets of the universe.

nodes.name: Counting MSO (CMSO)
nodes.statement:
We also use \defd{counting \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace} (\defd{\CMSO}), which is the extension of~$\ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace$ with, for every positive integer~$p$, a
unary set predicate~$\C[p]$ that checks whether the size of a subset is divisible by~$p$ or not. We only use~$\C[2]$.

nodes.name: Free variables of a formula
nodes.statement:
For a formula~$\phi$, we write, {\em e.g.},~$\phi(x,y,X)$ to indicate that the variables~$x$, $y$, and~$X$ belong to the set of \defd{free variables of~$\phi$},
namely, the set of variables occurring in~$\phi$ that are not bound to a quantifier within~$\phi$.

nodes.name: Sentence
nodes.statement: A \defd{sentence} is a formula without free variables.

nodes.name: Graphs as {edge}-structures
nodes.statement:
To model both graphs, unrooted trees, and directed graphs,
        we use the relational vocabulary~$\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$
        where~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace$ is a relation name of arity~$2$.
        A (directed) graph~$G=(V,E)$ is modeled
        as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}$
        with universe~$U_{\mathbb{G}}=V$
        and interpretation~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace_{\mathbb{G}}=E$.
        In particular if~$G$ is undirected, then $\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace_{\mathbb{G}}$ is symmetric.

nodes.name: Rooted trees as {ancestor}-structures
nodes.statement:
We use the relational vocabulary~$\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$ to model rooted trees
        where $\mathsf{ancestor}$ is a relation name of arity~$2$.
        A rooted tree~$T$ is modeled
        as the $\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$
        with universe~$U_{\mathbb{T}}=V(T)$
        and the interpretation~$\mathsf{ancestor}_{\mathbb{T}}$
        being the set of pairs~$(u,v)$ such that~$u$ is an ancestor of $v$ in $T$.
        It is routine to define \ensuremath{\operatorname{FO}}\xspace-formulas over this vocabulary
        to express the binary relations parent, child, proper ancestor, (proper) descendant,
        as well as the unary relations leaf and root.

nodes.name: Set systems as {SET}-structures
nodes.statement:
To model set systems, we use the extended vocabulary~$\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$
        where $\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$ is a set predicate name of arity~$1$.
        A set system~$S=(U,\mathcal{S})$ is thus naturally modeled
        as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{S}$
        with universe~$U_{\mathbb{S}}=U$
        and interpretation~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace_{\mathbb{S}}=\mathcal{S}$.

nodes.name: Sigma-to-Gamma transduction
nodes.statement:
Let~$\Sigma$ and~$\Gamma$ be two extended vocabularies.
A \defd{$\Sigma$-to-$\Gamma$ transduction}
is a set~$\tau$ of pairs formed by
a $\Sigma$-structure, call the \defd{input},
and a $\Gamma$-structure, called the \defd{output}.
We write \defd{$\mathbb{B}\in\tau(\mathbb{A})$} when~$(\mathbb{A},\mathbb{B})\in\tau$.

nodes.name: Overlay transduction
nodes.statement:
When for every pair~$(\mathbb{A},\mathbb{B})\in\tau$
we have~$\mathbb{A}\sqsubseteq\mathbb{B}$,
we call~$\tau$ an
\defd{overlay transduction}.

nodes.name: L-transduction (MSO- and CMSO[2]-transduction)
nodes.statement:
Some transductions
can be defined by means of \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace- or \CMSO[2]-formulas.
This leads to the notion of \defd{\ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-} and \defd{\CMSO[2]-transductions}.
Following the presentation of~\cite{BojanczykGP21},
for~$\mathsf{L}$ denoting~\ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace or~\CMSO[2],
define an \defd{$\mathsf{L}$-transduction}
to be a transduction obtained
by composing a finite number of \defd{atomic $\mathsf{L}$-transductions}
of the following kinds.
\begin{description}[nosep]
    \item[Filtering]
        An overlay transduction
        specified by an $\mathsf{L}$-sentence~$\phi$ over the input vocabulary~$\Sigma$,
        which discards the inputs that do not satisfy~$\phi$
        and keeps the other unchanged.
        Hence, it defines a partial function
        (actually, a partial identity)
        from $\Sigma$-structures to $\Sigma$-structures.
    \item[Universe restriction]
        A transduction specified by a $\mathsf{L}$-formula~$\phi$ over the input vocabulary~$\Sigma$,
        with one free first-order variable,
        which restricts the universe to those elements that satisfy~$\phi$.
        The output vocabulary is~$\Sigma$
        and the interpretation of every relation (resp.\xspace every predicate) in the output structure
        is defined as the restriction of its interpretation in the input structure
        to those tuples of elements satisfying~$\phi$ (resp.\xspace tuples of sets of elements that satisfy~$\phi$).
        This defines a total function from $\Sigma$-structures to $\Sigma$-structures.
    \item[Interpretation]
        A transduction specified by a family~$(\phi_Q)_{Q\in\Gamma}$ over the input vocabulary~$\Sigma$
        where~$\Gamma$ is the output vocabulary and each~$\phi_Q$ has $\operatorname{ar}(Q)$ free variables
        which are first-order if~$Q$ is a relation name and monadic if it is a set predicate name.
        The transduction outputs the~$\Gamma$-structure
        that has the same universe as the input structure
        and in which each relation or predicate~$Q$ is interpreted
        as those set of tuples that satisfy~$\phi_Q$.
        This defines a total function from $\Sigma$-structures to $\Gamma$-structures.
    \item[Copying]
        An overlay transduction parametrized by a positive integer~$k$ that
        adds $k$ copies of each element to the universe.
        The output vocabulary consists in the input vocabulary~$\Sigma$
        extended with~$k$ binary relational symbols~$(\copyV[i])_{i\in[k]}$
        interpreted as pairs of elements~$(x,y)$
        saying that ``$y$ is the $i$-th copy of~$x$''.
        The interpretation of the relations (resp.\xspace predicates) of the input structure
        are preserved, on original elements.
        This defines a total function from~$\Sigma$-structures to~$\Gamma$-structures,
        where~$\Gamma=\Sigma\cup\{\copyV[i]\mid i\in[k]\}$.
    \item[Colouring]
        An overlay transduction that adds a new unary relation~$\colorV\notin\Sigma$ to the structure.
        Any possible interpretation yields an output;
        indeed the interpretation is chosen non-deterministically.
        The interpretation of the relations (resp.\xspace predicates) of the input structure
        are preserved.
        Hence, it defines a total (non-functional) relation
        from $\Sigma$-structures to~$\Gamma$-structures
        where~$\Gamma=\Sigma\cup\{\colorV\}$ (providing $\colorV\notin\Sigma$).
nodes.statement_short: Compositions of finitely many atomic L-transductions: filtering, universe restriction, interpretation, copying, and colouring.

nodes.name: Deterministic and non-deterministic L-transductions
nodes.statement:
We say an $\mathsf{L}$-transduction is \defd{deterministic} if it does not use colouring,
it is \defd{non-deterministic} otherwise.
By definition, deterministic $\mathsf{L}$-transductions define functions.

nodes.name: CMSO[2]-transduction of the laminar tree
nodes.statement:
Let~$\Sigma$ be an extended vocabulary,
    including a unary set predicate name~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$
    and not including the binary relational symbol~$\mathsf{ancestor}$.
    There exists a non-deterministic \CMSO[2]-transduction~$\tau$
    such that,
    for each laminar set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
    represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure~$\mathbb{S}$
    and inducing the laminar tree~$T$ with ${L(T)=U}$,
    and for each $\Sigma$-structure~$\mathbb{A}$
    with~$\mathbb{S}\sqsubseteq\mathbb{A}$,
    $\tau(\mathbb{A})$ is non-empty
    and every output in~$\tau(\mathbb{A})$
    is equal to some $\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$ representing~$T$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-deterministic CMSO[2]-transduction outputs the laminar tree of any laminar set system embedded in a larger structure.
assumptions:
Let~$\Sigma$ be an extended vocabulary,
    including a unary set predicate name~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$
    and not including the binary relational symbol~$\mathsf{ancestor}$.

for each laminar set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
    represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure~$\mathbb{S}$
    and inducing the laminar tree~$T$ with ${L(T)=U}$

for each $\Sigma$-structure~$\mathbb{A}$
    with~$\mathbb{S}\sqsubseteq\mathbb{A}$
conclusions:
$\tau(\mathbb{A})$ is non-empty
    and every output in~$\tau(\mathbb{A})$
    is equal to some $\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$ representing~$T$.
nodes.label: thm:transduce laminar tree

nodes.name: Inverse MSO-transduction from the laminar tree to the set system
nodes.statement:
Since the sets from~$\mathcal{S}$
are precisely the sets of leaves of the subtrees of~$T$,
there is an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-transduction
which is the inverse of the above \CMSO[2]-transduction;
that is to say, given an $\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure~$\mathbb{T}$ representing the laminar tree, it
outputs the original set system~$\mathbb{S}$.
Namely,
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item An interpretation $\Phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace}(S)$
    that is true for a set $S$ when there exists an element $a$ such that an element $x$ is in $S$ if and only if $a$ is an ancestor of $x$.
    \item The filtering $\phi(x)$ keeping leaves only.
nodes.statement_short: An MSO-transduction recovers the set system from its laminar tree: sets are leaf sets of subtrees.
assumptions:
the sets from~$\mathcal{S}$
are precisely the sets of leaves of the subtrees of~$T$
conclusions:
there is an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-transduction
which is the inverse of the above \CMSO[2]-transduction

nodes.name: Fixed rooted tree T with node set V and leaf set L
nodes.statement:
We fix a rooted tree~$T$,\xspace
in which every inner node has at least two children (a necessary assumption that is satisfied by laminar trees),
and we let~$V$ denote the set of its nodes ($V=V(T)$)
and~$L\subseteq V$ denote the subset of its leaves ($L=L(T)$).

nodes.name: Pair of injections identifying a set of inner nodes
nodes.statement:
Let~$S\subseteq V\setminus L$,
and let~$(\pi,\sigma)$ be a pair of injective mappings from~$S$ to~$L$.
We say that the pair~$(\pi,\sigma)$ \emph{identifies~$S$}
if for each~$s\in S$, $s$ is the least common ancestor of~$\pi(s)$ and~$\sigma(s)$.
nodes.statement_short: (pi, sigma) identifies S when every s in S is the least common ancestor of its two leaves pi(s) and sigma(s).

nodes.name: s-requested node
nodes.statement:
For~$s\in S$ and~$x\in V$,
we say that~$x$ is \emph{$s$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$}
if~$x$ lies on the path from~$\pi(s)$ to~$\sigma(s)$
(namely, on either of the paths from~$\pi(s)$ to~$s$ and from~$\sigma(s)$ to~$s$).

nodes.name: Requested node
nodes.statement: We say that~$x$ is \emph{requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$} if it is $s$-requested for some~$s$.

nodes.name: Unique request
Unique request implies disjoint paths
nodes.statement: Note that if $(\pi,\sigma)$ has unique request then the paths from $\pi(s)$ to $\sigma(s)$ are pairwise disjoint for all the $s\in S$.
assumptions: $(\pi,\sigma)$ has unique request
conclusions: the paths from $\pi(s)$ to $\sigma(s)$ are pairwise disjoint for all the $s\in S$

nodes.name: Basic observations on identifying pairs
nodes.statement:
Let~$(\pi,\sigma)$ identifying some subset~$S$ of~$V\setminus L$.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The reversed pair $(\sigma,\pi)$ also identifies~$S$
            and has unique request whenever~$(\pi,\sigma)$ does.
        \item If~$S'\subset S$, then $(\pi_{|S'},\sigma_{|S'})$ identifies~$S'$,
            and has unique request if~$(\pi, \sigma)$ does.
        \item For each~$s\in S$, $s$ is $s$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$.
        \item If $(\sigma,\pi)$ has unique request,
            then~$\pi(S)$ and~$\sigma(S)$ are disjoint subsets of~$L$.
    \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Identification and unique request are preserved by swapping pi and sigma and by restriction; each s is s-requested; images are disjoint.
nodes.label: rk:identification basic observations

nodes.name: Representatives determine their node
nodes.statement:
Let~$(\pi,\sigma)$ identifying some subset~$S$ of~$V\setminus L$ with unique request.
    Then for each~$a\in\pi(S)$ 
    the node~$\pi^{-1}(a)$ 
    is the least ancestor of~$a$ 
    which belongs to~$S$.
assumptions: Let~$(\pi,\sigma)$ identifying some subset~$S$ of~$V\setminus L$ with unique request.
conclusions:
for each~$a\in\pi(S)$ 
    the node~$\pi^{-1}(a)$ 
    is the least ancestor of~$a$ 
    which belongs to~$S$.
nodes.label: lem:a reprensants

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement:
Let~$a\in\pi(S)$ and let~$s=\pi^{-1}(a)$.
    By definition, $s$ is an ancestor of~$a$ which belongs to~$S$.
    Let~$y$ be the least ancestor of $a$ that is contained in $S$. As $s$ is an ancestor of $a$ belonging to $S$, $y$ must be a descendant of $s$. Hence, $y$ is $s$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$. Additionally, by \autoref{rk:identification basic observations:self-request} of \autoref{rk:identification basic observations},
    $y$ is $y$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$.
    Since~$(\pi,\sigma)$ has unique request, $y=s$.
    Thus, $s$ is the least ancestor of~$a$ which belongs to~$S$.
nodes.statement_short: Let y be the least ancestor of a in S; y is both s-requested and y-requested, so unique request forces y = s.

nodes.name: Introduce a and s
nodes.statement:
Let~$a\in\pi(S)$ and let~$s=\pi^{-1}(a)$.
    By definition, $s$ is an ancestor of~$a$ which belongs to~$S$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a in pi(S) and its preimage s, an ancestor of a in S.

nodes.name: Least ancestor y is s-requested
nodes.statement: Let~$y$ be the least ancestor of $a$ that is contained in $S$. As $s$ is an ancestor of $a$ belonging to $S$, $y$ must be a descendant of $s$. Hence, $y$ is $s$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the least ancestor y of a in S; it lies on the path from a to s, so is s-requested.

nodes.name: Unique request gives y = s
nodes.statement:
Additionally, by \autoref{rk:identification basic observations:self-request} of \autoref{rk:identification basic observations},
    $y$ is $y$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$.
    Since~$(\pi,\sigma)$ has unique request, $y=s$.
nodes.statement_short: y is also y-requested (Remark 3.2), so unique request yields y = s.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, $s$ is the least ancestor of~$a$ which belongs to~$S$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence s is the least ancestor of a in S.

nodes.name: Identifying pairs are determined by their images
nodes.statement:
Let~$S\subseteq V\setminus L$,
    and $(\pi,\sigma)$ and $(\pi',\sigma')$
    be two pairs of injections from~$S$ to~$L$
    identifying~$S$ with unique request.
    If~$\pi(S)=\pi'(S)$ and~$\sigma(S)=\sigma'(S)$
    then $\pi=\pi'$ and~$\sigma=\sigma'$.
assumptions:
Let~$S\subseteq V\setminus L$,
    and $(\pi,\sigma)$ and $(\pi',\sigma')$
    be two pairs of injections from~$S$ to~$L$
    identifying~$S$ with unique request.
$\pi(S)=\pi'(S)$ and~$\sigma(S)=\sigma'(S)$
conclusions: $\pi=\pi'$ and~$\sigma=\sigma'$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement:
Let~$s\in S$, $a=\pi(s)$, and~$s'=\pi'^{-1}(a)$.
    Both~$s$ and~$s'$ are the least ancestor of~$a$ which belongs to~$S$,
    hence~$s=s'$ and~$\pi'(s)=a$.
    Thus~$\pi=\pi'$.
    By \autoref{rk:identification basic observations:commute} of \autoref{rk:identification basic observations},
    we also obtain that~$\sigma=\sigma'$.
nodes.statement_short: Both s and pi'^{-1}(pi(s)) are the least ancestor of pi(s) in S (Lemma 3.3), so pi = pi'; symmetrically sigma = sigma'.

nodes.name: pi equals pi'
nodes.statement:
Let~$s\in S$, $a=\pi(s)$, and~$s'=\pi'^{-1}(a)$.
    Both~$s$ and~$s'$ are the least ancestor of~$a$ which belongs to~$S$,
    hence~$s=s'$ and~$\pi'(s)=a$.
    Thus~$\pi=\pi'$.
nodes.statement_short: Both s and s' are the least ancestor of a in S, so pi = pi'.

nodes.name: Symmetric argument for sigma
nodes.statement:
By \autoref{rk:identification basic observations:commute} of \autoref{rk:identification basic observations},
    we also obtain that~$\sigma=\sigma'$.
nodes.statement_short: Swapping roles (Remark 3.2) gives sigma = sigma'.

nodes.name: Bi-colouring
nodes.statement:
Let~$A$ and~$B$ be two disjoint subsets of~$L$.
We call such a pair~$(A, B)$ a \emph{bi-colouring}.

nodes.name: Bi-colouring identifying a set
Three cases of inner nodes under an identifying bi-colouring
nodes.statement:
Let~$(A,B)$ identify some subset~$S$ of~$V\setminus L$
    through a pair~$(\pi,\sigma)$ of injections having unique request.
    Then,
    for each inner node~$x$,
    exactly one of the three following cases holds:

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement:
Let~$x$ be an inner node.
    We consider the set~$S'=S\setminus(V(T_x)\setminus\{x\})$ of all nodes which are not proper descendants of $x$
    and the restrictions~$\pi'$ and~$\sigma'$ of, respectively,~$\pi$ and~$\sigma$ to~$S'$.
    By \autoref{rk:identification basic observations:sub} of \autoref{rk:identification basic observations}
    $(\pi',\sigma')$ identify~$S'$ with unique request.
    We denote~$A'=\pi'(S')$ and~$B'=\sigma'(S')$, thus~$(A',B')$ identify~$S'$.
    Let $A'_x=A'\cap V(T_x)$ and $B'_x=B'\cap V(T_x)$ be the sets of representatives contained in $T_x$ of nodes in $S'$.
    Let~$a$ be an element of~$A'_x$.
    The element~$s_a=\pi^{-1}(a)$ is an ancestor of~$x$
    because it is an ancestor of~$a\in V(T_x)$
    and belongs to~$S'$ whence not to~$V(T_x)\setminus\{x\}$.
    Therefore,~$x$ is~$s_a$-requested.
    As~$(\pi',\sigma')$ has unique request,
    there exists at most one element in~$A'_x$.
    Similarly, $B'_x$ has size at most~$1$.
    Moreover, $A'_x\cap B'_x=\emptyset$
    by~\autoref{rk:identification basic observations:disjoint} of \autoref{rk:identification basic observations}.
    We thus we have three cases:
    \begin{description}
        \item[Case~$A'_x\cup B'_x=\emptyset$]
            Then there is no~$s\in S'$ such that~$\pi(s)\in V(T_x)$ or~$\sigma(s)\in V(T_x)$.
            Hence, $x$ is not requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$, in particular, $x\notin S$.

            Let~$c$ be a child of~$x$.
            If~$\card{A\cap V(T_{c})}\neq\card{B\cap V(T_c)}$,
            then there exists~$a\in(A\cup B)\cap V(T_{c})$
            such that,
            assuming without loss of generality that~$a\in A$ and denoting~$s_a=\pi^{-1}(a)$,
            $\sigma(s_a)\notin V(T_{c})$.
            Hence, $s_a$ is a proper ancestor of~$c$,
            thus, equivalently, an ancestor of~$x$,
            implying that~$x$ is $s_a$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$.
            This contradicts the above argument.
            So, $\card{A\cap V(T_c)}=\card{B\cap V(T_c)}$ for each child~$c$ of~$x$.
        \item[Case~$A'_x\cup B'_x=\{a\}$]
            Assume, without loss of generality, that~$a\in A$,
            and denote $s_a=\pi^{-1}(a)$ and~$b=\sigma(s_a)$.
            We have that~$s_a$ is a proper ancestor of~$x$,
            since it is the least common ancestor of~$a\in V(T_x)$ and~$b\notin V(T_x)$.
            Thus, $x$ is $s_a$-requested and~$s_a\neq x$ so~$x\notin S$.

            Let~$c$ be a child of~$x$.
            If~$\card{A\cap V(T_{c})}\neq\card{B\cap V(T_c)}$,
            then it means that there exists $z\in(A\cup B)\cap V(T_{c})$,
            such that
            either~$z\in A$ and $s_z=\pi^{-1}(z)\notin V(T_{c})$,
            or~$z\in B$ and~$s_z=\sigma^{-1}(z)\notin V(T_{c})$.
            In both cases, $s_z$ is a proper ancestor of~$c$,
            whence an ancestor of~$x$.
            Thus, $x$ is $s_z$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$.
            However, $x$ is $s_a$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$ which has unique request,
            hence~$s_z=s_a$.
            If~$z\in B$, it follows that~$z=b$, which contradicts the fact~$b\notin V(T_x)$.
            Hence, $z\in A$ and thus, $z=\pi(s_a)=a$.
            Therefore, $\card{(A\setminus\{a\})\cap V(T_{c})}=\card{B\cap V(T_c)}$
            for each child~$c$ of~$x$.
        \item[Case~$A'_x=\{a\}$ and~$B'_x=\{b\}$]
            Let~$s_a=\pi^{-1}(a)$ and~$s_b=\sigma^{-1}(b)$.
            The node $x$ is $s_a$-requested and $s_b$-requested in $(\pi,\sigma)$,
            so, by the unique request property, $s_a=s_b$.
            Since~$s_a$ is the least common ancestor of~$a$ and~$b$,
            it belongs to~$V(T_x)$
            whence~$s_a=x$ implying~$x\in X$.

            Let~$c$ be a child of~$x$.
            If~$\card{A\cap V(T_c)}\neq\card{B\cap V(T_c)}$,
            then there exists~$z\in (A\cup B)\cap V(T_{c})$
            such that either~$z\in A$ and~$s_z=\pi^{-1}(z)\notin V(T_{c})$,
            or~$z\in B$ and~$s_z=\sigma^{-1}(z)\notin V(T_{c})$.
            In both cases, $s_z$ is a proper ancestor of~$c$,
            whence an ancestor of~$x$,
            and thus $x$ is $s_z$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$.
            However, $x$ is $x$-requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$ which has unique request,
            hence~$s_z=x$ and thus~$z\in\{a,b\}$.
            Therefore, $\card{(A\setminus\{a\})\cap V(T_{c})}=\card{(B\setminus\{b\})\cap V(T_c)}$
            for each child~$c$ of~$x$.
            Because the least common ancestor of~$a$ and~$b$ is~$x$,
            there is no child~$c$ of~$x$ containing both~$a$ and~$b$ as leaves,
            {\em i.e.}, $\{a,b\}\nsubseteq V(T_c)$.
    \end{description}
    This concludes the proof of the statement.

nodes.name: A bi-colouring identifies at most one set
nodes.statement:
Let~$(A,B)$ be two disjoint subsets of~$L$
    and let~$S$ and~$S'$ be two subsets of~$V\setminus L$.
    If~$(A,B)$ identify both~$S$ and~$S'$, then~$S=S'$.
assumptions:
Let~$(A,B)$ be two disjoint subsets of~$L$
    and let~$S$ and~$S'$ be two subsets of~$V\setminus L$.
$(A,B)$ identify both~$S$ and~$S'$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement:
We proceed by contradiction and thus assume~$S\neq S'$.
    Let~$s\in S\setminus S'$.
    By \autoref{lem:node cases in identification},
    the number of children~$c$ of~$s$
    for which the set~$(A\cup B)\cap V(T_{c})$ has odd size is~$2$ since~$s\in S$,
    while it should also be less than~$2$ since~$s\notin S'$.
    A contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a node in S but not S' would have exactly two and fewer than two children with odd-size coloured subtrees (Lemma 3.5).

nodes.name: Assume S differs from S'
nodes.statement:
We proceed by contradiction and thus assume~$S\neq S'$.
    Let~$s\in S\setminus S'$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume S != S' and pick s in S \ S'.

nodes.name: Parity contradiction
nodes.statement:
By \autoref{lem:node cases in identification},
    the number of children~$c$ of~$s$
    for which the set~$(A\cup B)\cap V(T_{c})$ has odd size is~$2$ since~$s\in S$,
    while it should also be less than~$2$ since~$s\notin S'$.
    A contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.5 gives two odd children for s in S but fewer for s not in S'.

nodes.name: A-representative and B-representative
nodes.statement:
When~$(A,B)$ identifies a set~$S$,
we call \emph{$A$-representative} (resp.\xspace \emph{$B$-representative}) of~$s\in S$
the leaf~$\pi(s)\in A$ (resp.\xspace $\sigma(s)\in B$),
where~$(\pi,\sigma)$ witnessing that~$(A,B)$ identifies~$S$.

nodes.name: Thin set of inner nodes
nodes.statement:
A subset~$X\subseteq V\setminus L$ is \emph{thin}
when, for each~$x\in X$ not being the root,
on the one hand, the parent~$p_x$ of~$x$ does not belong to~$X$,
and on the other hand, $x$ admits at least one sibling (including possible leaves) that does not belong to~$X$.
differentia: the parent~$p_x$ of~$x$ does not belong to~$X$
$x$ admits at least one sibling (including possible leaves) that does not belong to~$X$

nodes.name: Thin sets admit avoiding branches
nodes.statement:
Let~$X\subseteq V\setminus L$ and~$s\in V\setminus X$.
    If~$X$ is thin, then there exists a leaf~$t\in V(T_s)$
    such that the path from~$t$ to~$s$ avoids~$X$
    ({\em i.e.}, none of the nodes along this path belong to~$X$).
assumptions: Let~$X\subseteq V\setminus L$ and~$s\in V\setminus X$.
$X$ is thin
conclusions:
there exists a leaf~$t\in V(T_s)$
    such that the path from~$t$ to~$s$ avoids~$X$
nodes.label: lem:thin => path avoiding

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.7
nodes.statement:
If~$T_s$ has height~$0$,
    then~$s$ is a leaf
    and taking~$t=s$ trivially gives the expected path.
    Otherwise,
    $s$ is an inner node and,
    because~$X$ is thin,
    $s$ has at least one child~$c_s$ not belonging to~$X$.
    By induction, there is a path from some leaf~$t\in V(T_{c_s})$ to~$c_s$ avoiding~$X$ and,
    since~$s\notin X$,
    this path could be extended into a path from~$t$ to~$s$ avoiding~$X$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the height of T_s: descend to a child not in X, which exists since X is thin.

nodes.name: Base case: s is a leaf
nodes.statement:
If~$T_s$ has height~$0$,
    then~$s$ is a leaf
    and taking~$t=s$ trivially gives the expected path.
nodes.statement_short: If s is a leaf, take t = s.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
Otherwise,
    $s$ is an inner node and,
    because~$X$ is thin,
    $s$ has at least one child~$c_s$ not belonging to~$X$.
    By induction, there is a path from some leaf~$t\in V(T_{c_s})$ to~$c_s$ avoiding~$X$ and,
    since~$s\notin X$,
    this path could be extended into a path from~$t$ to~$s$ avoiding~$X$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a child of s outside X and extend the inductively obtained path.

nodes.name: Thin sets are identifiable
nodes.statement:
If~$X$ is a thin set,
    then there exists a pair~$(\pi,\sigma)$
    of injections from~$X$ to~$L$
    that has unique request and that identifies~$X$.
assumptions: $X$ is a thin set
conclusions:
there exists a pair~$(\pi,\sigma)$
    of injections from~$X$ to~$L$
    that has unique request and that identifies~$X$.
nodes.label: lem:thin => identifiable

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.8
nodes.statement:
We proceed by induction on the size of~$X$.
    If~$X=\emptyset$, the result is trivial.
    Let~$n\in\mathbb{N}$ and suppose that for every thin set of size~$n$
    there exists a pair of injections identifying it with unique request.
    Let~$X$ be a thin set of size~$n+1$,
    and let~$s\in X$ be of minimal depth.
    Clearly, $X\setminus\{s\}$ is thin
    and thus there exists, by induction, a pair~$(\pi,\sigma)$
    of injections from~$X\setminus\{s\}$ to~$L$ identifying~$X\setminus\{s\}$ with unique request.
    Since~$X$ is thin and~$s\in X$,
    we can find two distinct children~$c_a$ and~$c_b$ of~$s$
    not belonging to~$X$.
    \footnote{ Remember that every inner node of~$T$ has at least two children (including possible leaves).}
    Then, by \autoref{lem:thin => path avoiding},
    there exists a leaf~$a\in V(T_{c_a})$ (resp.\xspace a leaf~$b\in V(T_{c_b})$)
    such that the path from~$a$ to~$c_a$ (resp.\xspace from~$b$ to~$c_b$)
    avoids~$X$.
    In particular, for each node~$y$ along these paths,
    since~$y$ has no ancestor that belongs to~$X$ but~$s$,
    $y$ is not requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$.
    Hence,
    extending~$\pi$ (resp.\xspace~$\sigma$) in such a way that,
    besides mapping each~$x\in X\setminus\{s\}$ to~$\pi(x)$ (resp.\xspace to~$\sigma(x)$),
    it maps~$s$ to~$a$ (resp.\xspace to~$b$),
    we obtain a pair~$(\hat{\pi},\hat{\sigma})$
    of injections from~$X$ to~$L$
    that identifies~$X$ with unique request.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on |X|: remove a minimal-depth node s, then map s to leaves reached by X-avoiding paths from two children not in X (Lemma 3.7).

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement:
We proceed by induction on the size of~$X$.
    If~$X=\emptyset$, the result is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on |X|; the empty set is trivial.

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis on X minus s
nodes.statement:
Let~$n\in\mathbb{N}$ and suppose that for every thin set of size~$n$
    there exists a pair of injections identifying it with unique request.
    Let~$X$ be a thin set of size~$n+1$,
    and let~$s\in X$ be of minimal depth.
    Clearly, $X\setminus\{s\}$ is thin
    and thus there exists, by induction, a pair~$(\pi,\sigma)$
    of injections from~$X\setminus\{s\}$ to~$L$ identifying~$X\setminus\{s\}$ with unique request.
nodes.statement_short: Remove a minimal-depth s; X \ {s} is thin and identified with unique request.

nodes.name: Two children outside X
nodes.statement:
Since~$X$ is thin and~$s\in X$,
    we can find two distinct children~$c_a$ and~$c_b$ of~$s$
    not belonging to~$X$.
    \footnote{ Remember that every inner node of~$T$ has at least two children (including possible leaves).}
nodes.statement_short: Thinness gives two distinct children c_a, c_b of s outside X.

nodes.name: Avoiding paths to leaves
nodes.statement:
Then, by \autoref{lem:thin => path avoiding},
    there exists a leaf~$a\in V(T_{c_a})$ (resp.\xspace a leaf~$b\in V(T_{c_b})$)
    such that the path from~$a$ to~$c_a$ (resp.\xspace from~$b$ to~$c_b$)
    avoids~$X$.
    In particular, for each node~$y$ along these paths,
    since~$y$ has no ancestor that belongs to~$X$ but~$s$,
    $y$ is not requested in~$(\pi,\sigma)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.7 gives leaves a, b via X-avoiding paths whose nodes are unrequested.

nodes.name: Extend the injections
nodes.statement:
Hence,
    extending~$\pi$ (resp.\xspace~$\sigma$) in such a way that,
    besides mapping each~$x\in X\setminus\{s\}$ to~$\pi(x)$ (resp.\xspace to~$\sigma(x)$),
    it maps~$s$ to~$a$ (resp.\xspace to~$b$),
    we obtain a pair~$(\hat{\pi},\hat{\sigma})$
    of injections from~$X$ to~$L$
    that identifies~$X$ with unique request.
nodes.statement_short: Map s to a and b to obtain an identifying pair with unique request.

nodes.name: Family of bi-colourings identifying a set
nodes.statement:
A family $F=(A_1,B_1),\ldots,(A_n,B_n)$ of bi-colourings
\emph{identifies} a set~$S\subseteq V\setminus L$,
if there exists a partition~$(S_1,\ldots,S_n)$ of~$S$
such that, for each~$i\in[n]$, $(A_i,B_i)$ identifies~$S_i$.

nodes.name: Family identifying T
nodes.statement: Whenever $S=V\setminus L$ we say that~$F$ \emph{identifies~$T$}.

nodes.name: Thin collection
nodes.statement:
A collection of subsets of~$V\setminus L$ is \emph{thin}
if each of its subsets is thin.

nodes.name: Thin 4-partition of inner nodes
nodes.statement: There exists a thin $4$-partition of~$V\setminus L$.
conclusions: There exists a thin $4$-partition of~$V\setminus L$.
nodes.label: lem:thin 4-partition

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.9
nodes.statement:
We build such a thin $4$-partition as follows.
    First, consider the partition~$(D_e,D_o)$ of~$V\setminus L$
    in which~$D_e$ (resp.\xspace $D_o=V\setminus(D_e\cup L)$) is the set of all inner nodes of even (resp.\xspace odd) depth.
    Second, arbitrarily fix one child~$c_x$ of~$x$ for each inner node~$x$,
    and consider the set~$C=\{ c_x \mid x\in V\setminus L \}\setminus L$,
    inducing a partition~$(C,\overline{C})$ of~$V\setminus L$ where~$\overline{C}=V\setminus(L\cup C)$.
    By refining these two bi-partitions, we obtain a $4$-partition which is thin by construction.
    \footref{fn:out-degree at least 2}
nodes.statement_short: Refine the even/odd-depth partition with the partition by a fixed chosen child of each inner node.

nodes.name: Depth-parity partition
nodes.statement:
We build such a thin $4$-partition as follows.
    First, consider the partition~$(D_e,D_o)$ of~$V\setminus L$
    in which~$D_e$ (resp.\xspace $D_o=V\setminus(D_e\cup L)$) is the set of all inner nodes of even (resp.\xspace odd) depth.
nodes.statement_short: Partition inner nodes by depth parity.

nodes.name: Chosen-child partition
nodes.statement:
Second, arbitrarily fix one child~$c_x$ of~$x$ for each inner node~$x$,
    and consider the set~$C=\{ c_x \mid x\in V\setminus L \}\setminus L$,
    inducing a partition~$(C,\overline{C})$ of~$V\setminus L$ where~$\overline{C}=V\setminus(L\cup C)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix one child per inner node and partition by membership in this set C.

nodes.name: Refine to a thin 4-partition
nodes.statement:
By refining these two bi-partitions, we obtain a $4$-partition which is thin by construction.
    \footref{fn:out-degree at least 2}
nodes.statement_short: The common refinement is a thin 4-partition.

nodes.name: Four bi-colourings identify T
nodes.statement: There exists a family of four bi-colourings identifying~$T$.
conclusions: There exists a family of four bi-colourings identifying~$T$.
nodes.label: cor:4 bi-colouring

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.10
nodes.statement: The result immediately follows from \autoref{lem:thin => identifiable} and \autoref{lem:thin 4-partition}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 3.8 with the thin 4-partition of Lemma 3.9.

nodes.name: MSO formulas desc and child on set systems
nodes.statement:
On $\mathbb{S}$,
we can define two \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formulas~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{desc}}\xspace(X,Y)$ and~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{child}}\xspace(X, Y)$
expressing that in the laminar tree induced by~$\mathcal{S}$,
$X$ and~$Y$ are nodes and~$X$ is a descendant or a child of~$Y$, respectively:
\begin{align*}
    \ensuremath{\mathsf{desc}}\xspace(X, Y)&:=
    \ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(X)\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(Y)\land X\subseteq Y;
    \\*
    \ensuremath{\mathsf{child}}\xspace(X, Y)&:=
    \ensuremath{\mathsf{desc}}\xspace(X, Y)\land X\neq Y\land
    \forall Z\:
    \Big(\big(
    \ensuremath{\mathsf{desc}}\xspace(Z, Y)
    \land
    Z\neq Y\big)
    \rightarrow
    \ensuremath{\mathsf{desc}}\xspace(Z, X)
    \Big).
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: MSO formulas expressing that X is a descendant, resp. child, of Y in the laminar tree of the set system.

nodes.name: CMSO[2]-definability of representatives
nodes.statement:
Let~$(A,B)$ be a bi-colouring of~$L(T)$
    identifying a subset~$S$ of inner nodes of~$T$.
    There exists a \CMSO[2]-formula~$\repr_{A,B}(a, X)$
    that is satisfied exactly
    when~$X$ is an inner node of~$T$
    that belongs to~$S$ and is $A$-represented by~$a$.
nodes.statement_short: Given a bi-colouring identifying S, a CMSO[2]-formula repr_{A,B}(a, X) holds exactly when X is in S with A-representative a.
assumptions:
Let~$(A,B)$ be a bi-colouring of~$L(T)$
    identifying a subset~$S$ of inner nodes of~$T$.
conclusions:
There exists a \CMSO[2]-formula~$\repr_{A,B}(a, X)$
    that is satisfied exactly
    when~$X$ is an inner node of~$T$
    that belongs to~$S$ and is $A$-represented by~$a$.
nodes.label: lem:repr MSO

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.11
nodes.statement:
First, we define a formula~$\phi_{A,B}(X)$
    that, under the above assumption,
    is satisfied exactly when~$X$ belongs to~$S$.
    According to~\autoref{lem:node cases in identification},
    this happens if and only if\xspace
    $X$ is a node of~$T$
    ({\em i.e.},~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(X)$ is satisfied)
    and there exists~$a\in X\cap A$ and~$b\in X\cap B$
    such that for each child~$Z$ of~$X$,
    $\{a,b\}\nsubseteq Z$
    and
    the set~$(Z\setminus\{a,b\})\cap(A\cup B)$ has even size.
    This property is easily expressed in \CMSO[2],
    using the \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula $\ensuremath{\mathsf{child}}\xspace(X, Y)$ defined previously,
    as well as the predicate $\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$:
    \begin{align*}
        \phi_{A,B}(X):=\:
        &
        \ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(X)
        \land
        \exists a\exists b\Big[a\in (X\cap A)\land b\in (X\cap B)\land
        \\*&\qquad
        \forall Z\:
        \Big(
        \ensuremath{\mathsf{child}}\xspace(Z, X) \rightarrow \Big(
        \{a,b\}\nsubseteq Z
        \land
        \C[2]\big((Z\setminus\{a,b\})\cap(A\cup B)\big)
        \Big)\Big)\Big].
    \end{align*}

    Now, we can easily define~$\repr_{A,B}(a, X)$
    based on \autoref{lem:a reprensants}:
    \begin{align*}
        \repr_{A,B}(a, X):=\:&
        \phi_{A,B}(X) \land a\in (X\cap A)
        \land
        \forall Z\subsetneq X\:
        \Big(
        a\in Z
        \rightarrow \neg \phi_{A,B}(Z)
        \Big).
    \end{align*}
    This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Define phi_{A,B}(X) via the parity characterisation of Lemma 3.5, then repr_{A,B} picks the least such X containing a (Lemma 3.3).

nodes.name: Formula selecting S
nodes.statement:
First, we define a formula~$\phi_{A,B}(X)$
    that, under the above assumption,
    is satisfied exactly when~$X$ belongs to~$S$.
    According to~\autoref{lem:node cases in identification},
    this happens if and only if\xspace
    $X$ is a node of~$T$
    ({\em i.e.},~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(X)$ is satisfied)
    and there exists~$a\in X\cap A$ and~$b\in X\cap B$
    such that for each child~$Z$ of~$X$,
    $\{a,b\}\nsubseteq Z$
    and
    the set~$(Z\setminus\{a,b\})\cap(A\cup B)$ has even size.
    This property is easily expressed in \CMSO[2],
    using the \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula $\ensuremath{\mathsf{child}}\xspace(X, Y)$ defined previously,
    as well as the predicate $\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$:
    \begin{align*}
        \phi_{A,B}(X):=\:
        &
        \ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(X)
        \land
        \exists a\exists b\Big[a\in (X\cap A)\land b\in (X\cap B)\land
        \\*&\qquad
        \forall Z\:
        \Big(
        \ensuremath{\mathsf{child}}\xspace(Z, X) \rightarrow \Big(
        \{a,b\}\nsubseteq Z
        \land
        \C[2]\big((Z\setminus\{a,b\})\cap(A\cup B)\big)
        \Big)\Big)\Big].
    \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Using Lemma 3.5, express membership in S by a C_2 parity condition on children.

nodes.name: Formula for representatives
nodes.statement:
Now, we can easily define~$\repr_{A,B}(a, X)$
    based on \autoref{lem:a reprensants}:
    \begin{align*}
        \repr_{A,B}(a, X):=\:&
        \phi_{A,B}(X) \land a\in (X\cap A)
        \land
        \forall Z\subsetneq X\:
        \Big(
        a\in Z
        \rightarrow \neg \phi_{A,B}(Z)
        \Big).
    \end{align*}
    This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.3, a represents the minimal X in S containing it.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
The \CMSO[2]-transduction is obtained by composing the following atomic \CMSO[2]-transductions.
    The transduction makes use of the formulas~$\repr_{A, B}(a, X)$
    given by \autoref{lem:repr MSO}.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Guess a family of four bi-colourings~$(A_i, B_i)_{i\in[4]}$
            identifying~$T$
            (which exists by \autoref{cor:4 bi-colouring}).
        \item Copy the input graph four times,
            thus introducing four binary relations~$(\copyV[i])_{i\in[4]}$
            where $\copyV[i](x, y)$ indicates that~$x$ is the $i$-th copy
            of the original element~$y$.
        \item Filter the universe
            keeping only
            the original elements
            as well as
            the $i$-th copy of each vertex~$a$
            for which there exists~$X$
            such that~$\repr_{A_i, B_i}(a, X)$.
        \item Define the relation~$\mathsf{ancestor}(x, y)$
            so that it is satisfied exactly when
            there exist~$x'$, $X$, $i$, and~$Y$
            such that,
            on the one hand
            $\ensuremath{\mathsf{desc}}\xspace(Y, X)$
            and
            $\copyV[i](x,x')\land\repr_{A_i, B_i}(x', X)$,
            and,
            on the other hand,
            either~$y$ is an original element and~$Y=\{y\}$,
            or there exists~$y'$ and~$j$ such that
            $\copyV[j](y, y')\land\repr_{A_j, B_j}(y', Y)$.
    \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Guess four identifying bi-colourings, copy the universe four times, keep representatives, and define ancestor via repr formulas.

nodes.name: Composition of atomic transductions
nodes.statement:
The \CMSO[2]-transduction is obtained by composing the following atomic \CMSO[2]-transductions.
    The transduction makes use of the formulas~$\repr_{A, B}(a, X)$
    given by \autoref{lem:repr MSO}.
    \begin{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The transduction composes atomic steps using repr from Lemma 3.11.

nodes.name: Guess bi-colourings
nodes.statement:
Guess a family of four bi-colourings~$(A_i, B_i)_{i\in[4]}$
            identifying~$T$
            (which exists by \autoref{cor:4 bi-colouring}).
nodes.statement_short: Guess four bi-colourings identifying T (Corollary 3.10).

nodes.name: Copy four times
nodes.statement:
Copy the input graph four times,
            thus introducing four binary relations~$(\copyV[i])_{i\in[4]}$
            where $\copyV[i](x, y)$ indicates that~$x$ is the $i$-th copy
            of the original element~$y$.
nodes.statement_short: Copy the input four times.

nodes.name: Filter to representatives
nodes.statement:
Filter the universe
            keeping only
            the original elements
            as well as
            the $i$-th copy of each vertex~$a$
            for which there exists~$X$
            such that~$\repr_{A_i, B_i}(a, X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Keep originals and copies representing inner nodes.

nodes.name: Define ancestor
nodes.statement:
Define the relation~$\mathsf{ancestor}(x, y)$
            so that it is satisfied exactly when
            there exist~$x'$, $X$, $i$, and~$Y$
            such that,
            on the one hand
            $\ensuremath{\mathsf{desc}}\xspace(Y, X)$
            and
            $\copyV[i](x,x')\land\repr_{A_i, B_i}(x', X)$,
            and,
            on the other hand,
            either~$y$ is an original element and~$Y=\{y\}$,
            or there exists~$y'$ and~$j$ such that
            $\copyV[j](y, y')\land\repr_{A_j, B_j}(y', Y)$.
    \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Define ancestor via desc and repr formulas.

nodes.name: Weakly-partitive set system
differentia: for every two overlapping sets~$X,Y\in\mathcal{S}$, the sets~$X\cup Y$, $X\cap Y$, $X\setminus Y$, and~$Y\setminus X$ belong to~$\mathcal{S}$

nodes.name: Partitive set system and symmetric difference
nodes.statement:
It is \defd{partitive} if, moreover,
for every two overlapping sets~$X,Y\in\mathcal{S}$,
their symmetric difference, denoted \defd{$X\bigtriangleup Y$},
also belongs to~$\mathcal{S}$.

nodes.name: Weakly-partitive and partitive set families
nodes.statement:
By extension, a set family~$\mathcal{S}$ is called \defd{weakly-partitive} or \defd{partitive}
whenever $\left(\bigcup\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}\right)$ is a set system\xspace
which is weakly-partitive or partitive, respectively
(note these also requires that~$\emptyset\notin\mathcal{S}$, $\bigcup\mathcal{S}\in\mathcal{S}$, and~$\{a\}\in\mathcal{S}$ for every~$a\in\bigcup\mathcal{S}$).

nodes.name: Strong member of a set system
nodes.statement:
A member of a set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$ is said to be~\defd{strong}
if it does not overlap any other set from~$\mathcal{S}$.
differentia: does not overlap any other set from~$\mathcal{S}$

nodes.name: Family of strong sets
nodes.statement: The sub-family~\defd{$\mathcal{S}_!$} of strong sets of~$\mathcal{S}$ is thus laminar by definition.

nodes.name: Laminar tree induced by a set system
nodes.statement:
Hence, it induces a laminar tree~$T$.
By extension,
we say that~$T$ is \defd{induced by the set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$} (or simply by~$\mathcal{S}$).

nodes.name: CMSO[2]-transduction of the laminar tree induced by a set system
nodes.statement:
Let~$\Sigma$ be an extended vocabulary,
    including a set unary predicate name~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$
    and not including the binary relational symbol~$\mathsf{ancestor}$.
    There exists a non-deterministic \CMSO[2]-transduction~$\tau$
    such that,
    for each set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
    represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure~$\mathbb{S}$
    and inducing the laminar tree~$T$ with ${L(T)=U}$,
    and for each $\Sigma$-structure~$\mathbb{A}$
    with~$\mathbb{S}\sqsubseteq\mathbb{A}$,
    $\tau(\mathbb{A})$ is non-empty
    and every output in~$\tau(\mathbb{A})$
    is equal to some $\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$ representing $T$.
nodes.statement_short: The laminar tree of the strong sets of any set system can be CMSO[2]-transduced from the set system.
assumptions:
Let~$\Sigma$ be an extended vocabulary,
    including a set unary predicate name~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$
    and not including the binary relational symbol~$\mathsf{ancestor}$.

for each set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
    represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure~$\mathbb{S}$
    and inducing the laminar tree~$T$ with ${L(T)=U}$

for each $\Sigma$-structure~$\mathbb{A}$
    with~$\mathbb{S}\sqsubseteq\mathbb{A}$
conclusions:
$\tau(\mathbb{A})$ is non-empty
    and every output in~$\tau(\mathbb{A})$
    is equal to some $\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$ representing $T$.
nodes.label: lem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-partitive family

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement:
On the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure~$\mathbb{S}$,
    it is routine to define an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula~$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace}(Z)$
    that identifies those subsets~$Z\subseteq U$
    that are strong members of~$\mathcal{S}$:
    \begin{align*}
        \phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace}(Z)&:=
        \ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(Z)
        \land
        \forall X\:
        \Big(
        \big( \ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(X) \land X\cap Z\neq\emptyset \big)
        \rightarrow
        \big( X\subseteq Z \lor Z\subseteq X \big)
        \Big).
    \end{align*}
    Hence, we can design an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-interpretation
    that outputs the $\Sigma\cup\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace\}$-structure
    corresponding to~$\mathbb{A}$ equipped with the set unary predicate $\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace$
    that selects strong members of~$\mathcal{S}$.
    Thus, up to renaming the predicates~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace$ and~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$,
    by \autoref{thm:transduce laminar tree},
    we can produce,
    through a \CMSO[2]-transduction,
    the $\Sigma\cup\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{A}\sqcup\mathbb{T}$
    where~$\mathbb{T}$ is the tree-structure modeling the laminar tree~$T$ induced by~$\mathcal{S}_!$
    with~$L(T)=U$
    (once the output obtained, the interpretation drops the set predicate~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace$ which is no longer needed).
nodes.statement_short: MSO-define the strong members as a new predicate SET!, then apply Theorem 3.1 to this laminar family.

nodes.name: Formula for strong members
nodes.statement:
On the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure~$\mathbb{S}$,
    it is routine to define an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula~$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace}(Z)$
    that identifies those subsets~$Z\subseteq U$
    that are strong members of~$\mathcal{S}$:
    \begin{align*}
        \phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace}(Z)&:=
        \ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(Z)
        \land
        \forall X\:
        \Big(
        \big( \ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(X) \land X\cap Z\neq\emptyset \big)
        \rightarrow
        \big( X\subseteq Z \lor Z\subseteq X \big)
        \Big).
    \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Strong members are MSO-definable by phi_SET!.

nodes.name: Interpretation adding SET!
nodes.statement:
Hence, we can design an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-interpretation
    that outputs the $\Sigma\cup\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace\}$-structure
    corresponding to~$\mathbb{A}$ equipped with the set unary predicate $\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace$
    that selects strong members of~$\mathcal{S}$.
nodes.statement_short: An MSO-interpretation adds the predicate SET! for strong members.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
Thus, up to renaming the predicates~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace$ and~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$,
    by \autoref{thm:transduce laminar tree},
    we can produce,
    through a \CMSO[2]-transduction,
    the $\Sigma\cup\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{A}\sqcup\mathbb{T}$
    where~$\mathbb{T}$ is the tree-structure modeling the laminar tree~$T$ induced by~$\mathcal{S}_!$
    with~$L(T)=U$
    (once the output obtained, the interpretation drops the set predicate~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET!}}\xspace$ which is no longer needed).
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1 applied to SET! produces the laminar tree.

nodes.name: <-interval
nodes.statement:
For~$Z$ a set equipped with a partial order~$<$
and~$X$ a subset of~$Z$,
we say that~$X$ is a \defd{$<$-interval}
whenever $<$ defines a total order on~$X$
and for every~$a,b\in X$ and every~$c\in Z$,
$a<c<b$ implies~$c\in X$.

nodes.name: Weakly-partitive tree theorem
nodes.statement:
Let~$\mathcal{S}$ be a weakly-partitive family,
    $\mathcal{S}_!$ be its subfamily of strong sets,
    and~$T$ be the laminar tree it induces.
    There exists a total labeling function~$\lambda$
    from the set~$V(T)\setminus L(T)$ of inner nodes of~$T$
    to the set~$\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{prime}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace\}$,
    and, for each inner node~$t\in\lambda^{-1}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace)$,
    a linear ordering~$<_t$ of its children,
    such that
    every inner node having exactly two children is labeled by~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$ and the following two conditions are satisfied:
    \begin{itemize}[nosep]
        \item for each~$X\in\mathcal{S}\setminus\mathcal{S}_!$,
            there exists~$t\in V(T)$
            and a subset~$\mathcal{C}$ of children of~$t$
            such that $X=\bigcup_{c\in\mathcal{C}}L(T_c)$
            and
            either~$\lambda(t)=\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace$
            and~$\mathcal{C}$ is a $<_t$-interval,
            or~$\lambda(t)=\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$;
        \item conversely,
            for each inner node~$t$
            and each non-empty subset~$\mathcal{C}$ of children of~$t$,
            if
            either~$\lambda(t)=\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace$
            and~$\mathcal{C}$ is a $<_t$-interval,
            or~$\lambda(t)=\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$,
            then~$\bigcup_{c\in\mathcal{C}}L(T_c)\in\mathcal{S}$.
    \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The strong-set laminar tree of a weakly-partitive family, with degenerate/prime/linear labels and child orders on linear nodes, describes all its sets.
also_stated_at: Roughly speaking, if a set system $(U,\mathcal{S})$ is well behaved, i.e. $(U,\mathcal{S})$ is weakly-partitive (definition in \autoref{sec:preliminaries}), then there is a labelling $\lambda$ of $T$ and a partial order $<$ of its nodes such that $(U,\mathcal{S})$ is completely described by $(T,\lambda,<)$ \cite{chein1981partitive,raoThesis}.
assumptions:
Let~$\mathcal{S}$ be a weakly-partitive family,
    $\mathcal{S}_!$ be its subfamily of strong sets,
    and~$T$ be the laminar tree it induces.
conclusions: There exists a total labeling function~$\lambda$

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the weakly-partitive tree
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, $T$ and $\lambda$ are uniquely determined from~$\mathcal{S}$,
and, for each inner node~$t$ of~$T$ labeled by~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace$, only two orders~$<_t$ are possible,
one being the inverse of the other
(indeed, inverting an order~$<$ does preserve the property of being a $<$-interval).
conclusions: $T$ and $\lambda$ are uniquely determined from~$\mathcal{S}$

only two orders~$<_t$ are possible,
one being the inverse of the other

nodes.name: Weakly-partitive tree induced by a family
nodes.statement:
Hence, every weakly-partitive family~$\mathcal{S}$ is characterized
by a labeled and partially-ordered tree~$(T,\lambda,<)$
where~$T$ is the laminar tree induced by the subfamily~$\mathcal{S}_!$ of strong sets of~$\mathcal{S}$,
$\lambda:V(T)\setminus L(T)\to\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{prime}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace\}$ is the labeling function,
and~$<$ is the partial order $\bigcup_{t\in\lambda^{-1}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace)}<_t$ over~$V(T)$.
As, up-to inverting some of the $<_t$ orders, $(T,\lambda,<)$ is unique,
we abusively call it \defd{\strong{the} weakly-partitive tree induced by~$\mathcal{S}$}.
nodes.statement_short: The labeled, partially-ordered tree (T, lambda, <) over the strong-set laminar tree, unique up to inverting the linear orders.

nodes.name: Weakly-partitive trees as {ancestor, degenerate, betweeness}-structures
nodes.statement:
We naturally model a weakly-partitive tree~$(T,\lambda,<)$ of a partitive set system $(U,\mathcal{S})$
by the $\{\mathsf{ancestor},\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace,\mathsf{betweeness}\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$
of universe $U_{\mathbb{T}}=V(T)$ such that
$\struct{V(T),\mathsf{ancestor}_{\mathbb{T}}}\sqsubseteq\mathbb{T}$ models~$T$ with ${L(T)=U}$,
$\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace_{\mathbb{T}}$ is a unary relation
which selects the inner nodes of~$T$ of label~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$,
{\em i.e.}, ${\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace_{\mathbb{T}}=\lambda^{-1}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace)}$,
and~$\mathsf{betweeness}_{\mathbb{T}}$ is a ternary relation selecting triples $(x,y,z)$ satisfying $x<y<z$ or $z<y<x$.
nodes.statement_short: Model a weakly-partitive tree by its ancestor relation, a unary degenerate predicate, and a ternary betweenness relation from the orders.

nodes.name: MSO-transduction from a weakly-partitive tree to its set system
nodes.statement:
Using \autoref{thm:weakly-partitive tree},
it is routine to design an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-transduction
which takes as input a weakly-partitive tree
and outputs the weakly-partitive set system which induced it.
conclusions:
it is routine to design an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-transduction
which takes as input a weakly-partitive tree
and outputs the weakly-partitive set system which induced it.

nodes.name: CMSO[2]-transduction of weakly-partitive trees
nodes.statement:
There exists a non-deterministic \CMSO[2]-transduction~$\tau$
    such that,
    for every weakly-partitive set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
    represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{S}$
    and inducing the weakly-partitive tree $(T,\lambda,<)$
    represented as the $\{\mathsf{ancestor},\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace,\mathsf{betweeness}\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$,
    we have $\mathbb{T}\in\tau(\mathbb{S})$
    and every output in $\tau(\mathbb{S})$ is a weakly-partitive tree of $(U,\mathcal{S})$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-deterministic CMSO[2]-transduction outputs the weakly-partitive tree of any weakly-partitive set system.
assumptions:
for every weakly-partitive set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
    represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{S}$
    and inducing the weakly-partitive tree $(T,\lambda,<)$
    represented as the $\{\mathsf{ancestor},\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace,\mathsf{betweeness}\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$
conclusions:
we have $\mathbb{T}\in\tau(\mathbb{S})$
    and every output in $\tau(\mathbb{S})$ is a weakly-partitive tree of $(U,\mathcal{S})$.
nodes.label: thm:transduce weakly-partitive tree

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement:
By \autoref{lem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-partitive family},
    we have a \CMSO[2]-transduction
    which on inputs~$\mathbb{S}$ outputs the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace,\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{S}\sqcup\mathbb{T'}$,
    where~$\mathbb{T'}$ is the~$\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure modeling~$T$, with $L(T)=U=U_{\mathbb{S}}$.
    It thus remains to define a second \CMSO[2]-transduction
    which outputs~$\mathbb{T}$ from~$\mathbb{S}\sqcup\mathbb{T'}$.
    Actually, an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-interpretation is enough.
    Indeed, we can define
    an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula~$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace}$ which selects the inner nodes of~$T$ that are labeled~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$ by~$\lambda$,
    and an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula~$\phi_{\mathsf{betweeness}}$ which selects triples~$(x,y,z)$ of elements such that~$x<y<z$ or~$z<y<x$.
    In order to define both formulas,
    we use a functional symbol~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(t)$
    which is interpreted as the set~$L(T_t)$,
    and is clearly \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-definable on~$\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structures such as~$\mathbb{T}$.
    Indeed, an element~$z$ belongs to~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(t)$ if and only if\xspace
    it is a leaf and has~$t$ as ancestor.

    According to \autoref{thm:weakly-partitive tree},
    an inner node~$t$ is labeled~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$
    if and only if\xspace,
    for every two children $s_1,s_2$ of $t$ the set $L(T_{s_1})\cup L(T_{s_2})$ is in $\mathcal{S}$. We can define this in \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace using the following formula:
        $$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace}(x):=\forall y \forall z\Big(\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(x,y)\land \ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(x,z)\big)\rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(y)\cup \ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\big)\Big).$$


    Now, according to \autoref{thm:weakly-partitive tree},
    we have~$x<y<z$ or~$z<y<x$ exactly when~$x$, $y$, and~$z$ are three distinct children of some node~$t$
    and the three following properties are satisfied:
    \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
        \item $L(T_x)\cup L(T_z)$ is not a member of~$\mathcal{S}$;
        \item  there exists a member of~$\mathcal{S}$ which includes both~$L(T_x)$ and~$L(T_y)$ but excludes~$L(T_z)$;
        \item  there exists a member of~$\mathcal{S}$ which includes both~$L(T_y)$ and~$L(T_z)$ but excludes~$L(T_x)$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Indeed,
    when these conditions are satisfied, $t$ is necessarily labeled $\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace$
    (\autoref{it:not degenerate} asserts that it is not labeled by $\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$ and, {\em e.g.}, \autoref{it:not prime} that it is not labeled by $\ensuremath{\mathsf{prime}}\xspace$),
    and, among the possible orderings of~$\{x,y,z\}$, only the ones ensuring~$x<y<z$ or~$z<y<x$ are possible
    ($x<z<y$ and~$y<z<x$ are not possible because of \autoref{it:x+y-z},
    and~$y<x<z$ and~$z<x<y$ are not possible because of \autoref{it:y+z-x}).
    Each of these properties is \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-definable:
    \begin{align*}
        \phi_{\mathsf{betweeness}}(x,y,z):=&
            \exists t\Big[ \ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(t,x)\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(t,y)\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(t,z)\land 
            \\*
            &\neg\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(x)\cup\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\big)\land
            \\*
            &\exists S\Big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(S)\land\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(x)\cup\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(y)\big)\subseteq S\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\cap S=\emptyset\Big)\land
            \\*
            &\exists S\Big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(S)\land\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\cup\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(y)\big)\subseteq S\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(x)\cap S=\emptyset\Big)\Big].
    \end{align*}
    Once~$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace}$ and~$\phi_{\mathsf{betweeness}}$ are defined,
    our transduction drops the original predicate~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$
    which is no longer needed in the output~$\mathbb{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Transduce the laminar tree by Lemma 4.1, then MSO-define the degenerate label and betweenness from Theorem 4.1's characterisation via leaf sets.

nodes.name: Laminar tree via Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement:
By \autoref{lem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-partitive family},
    we have a \CMSO[2]-transduction
    which on inputs~$\mathbb{S}$ outputs the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace,\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure $\mathbb{S}\sqcup\mathbb{T'}$,
    where~$\mathbb{T'}$ is the~$\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structure modeling~$T$, with $L(T)=U=U_{\mathbb{S}}$.
    It thus remains to define a second \CMSO[2]-transduction
    which outputs~$\mathbb{T}$ from~$\mathbb{S}\sqcup\mathbb{T'}$.
    Actually, an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-interpretation is enough.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.1 yields S together with the laminar tree; an MSO-interpretation remains.

nodes.name: Introduce formulas and leafset
nodes.statement:
Indeed, we can define
    an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula~$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace}$ which selects the inner nodes of~$T$ that are labeled~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$ by~$\lambda$,
    and an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula~$\phi_{\mathsf{betweeness}}$ which selects triples~$(x,y,z)$ of elements such that~$x<y<z$ or~$z<y<x$.
    In order to define both formulas,
    we use a functional symbol~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(t)$
    which is interpreted as the set~$L(T_t)$,
    and is clearly \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-definable on~$\{\mathsf{ancestor}\}$-structures such as~$\mathbb{T}$.
    Indeed, an element~$z$ belongs to~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(t)$ if and only if\xspace
    it is a leaf and has~$t$ as ancestor.
nodes.statement_short: Plan formulas for degenerate and betweeness, using an MSO-definable leafset function.

nodes.name: Define degenerate
nodes.statement_short: A node is degenerate iff every union of two child leaf sets is in S.

nodes.name: Characterise betweenness
nodes.statement_short: x<y<z or z<y<x iff three sibling conditions on S hold.

nodes.name: Statement of the three conditions
nodes.statement:
Now, according to \autoref{thm:weakly-partitive tree},
    we have~$x<y<z$ or~$z<y<x$ exactly when~$x$, $y$, and~$z$ are three distinct children of some node~$t$
    and the three following properties are satisfied:
    \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
nodes.statement_short: Betweenness holds exactly for three siblings satisfying the conditions below.

nodes.name: Condition 1
nodes.statement: $L(T_x)\cup L(T_z)$ is not a member of~$\mathcal{S}$;
nodes.statement_short: The union of the leaf sets of x and z is not in S.

nodes.name: Condition 2
nodes.statement: there exists a member of~$\mathcal{S}$ which includes both~$L(T_x)$ and~$L(T_y)$ but excludes~$L(T_z)$;
nodes.statement_short: Some set contains the leaves of x and y but not z.

nodes.name: Condition 3
nodes.statement:
there exists a member of~$\mathcal{S}$ which includes both~$L(T_y)$ and~$L(T_z)$ but excludes~$L(T_x)$.
    \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Some set contains the leaves of y and z but not x.

nodes.name: Justify conditions and define betweeness
nodes.statement:
Indeed,
    when these conditions are satisfied, $t$ is necessarily labeled $\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace$
    (\autoref{it:not degenerate} asserts that it is not labeled by $\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace$ and, {\em e.g.}, \autoref{it:not prime} that it is not labeled by $\ensuremath{\mathsf{prime}}\xspace$),
    and, among the possible orderings of~$\{x,y,z\}$, only the ones ensuring~$x<y<z$ or~$z<y<x$ are possible
    ($x<z<y$ and~$y<z<x$ are not possible because of \autoref{it:x+y-z},
    and~$y<x<z$ and~$z<x<y$ are not possible because of \autoref{it:y+z-x}).
    Each of these properties is \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-definable:
    \begin{align*}
        \phi_{\mathsf{betweeness}}(x,y,z):=&
            \exists t\Big[ \ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(t,x)\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(t,y)\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(t,z)\land 
            \\*
            &\neg\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(x)\cup\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\big)\land
            \\*
            &\exists S\Big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(S)\land\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(x)\cup\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(y)\big)\subseteq S\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\cap S=\emptyset\Big)\land
            \\*
            &\exists S\Big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace(S)\land\big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(z)\cup\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(y)\big)\subseteq S\land\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(x)\cap S=\emptyset\Big)\Big].
    \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The conditions force label linear and exclude other orderings; express them in MSO.

nodes.name: Drop SET
nodes.statement:
Once~$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace}$ and~$\phi_{\mathsf{betweeness}}$ are defined,
    our transduction drops the original predicate~$\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace$
    which is no longer needed in the output~$\mathbb{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Drop SET to output the tree structure.

nodes.name: Partitive families have no linear nodes
nodes.statement:
Let~$\mathcal{S}$ be a weakly-partitive family
    and~$(T,\lambda,<)$ be the weakly-partitive tree it induces.
    If~$\mathcal{S}$ is partitive,
    then~$\lambda^{-1}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace)=\emptyset$ and~$<$ is empty.
assumptions:
Let~$\mathcal{S}$ be a weakly-partitive family
    and~$(T,\lambda,<)$ be the weakly-partitive tree it induces.
$\mathcal{S}$ is partitive
conclusions: $\lambda^{-1}(\ensuremath{\mathsf{linear}}\xspace)=\emptyset$ and~$<$ is empty.

nodes.name: Partitive tree
nodes.statement:
Hence, in case of a partitive set systems~$(U,\mathcal{S})$,
we can consider the simpler object~$(T,\lambda)$,
called \defd{the partitive tree induced by~$\mathcal{S}$}
(or \defd{the partitive tree of~$(U,\mathcal{S})$})
in which~$\lambda$ maps $V(T)\setminus L(T)$ to $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{prime}}\xspace\}$.

nodes.name: Derivation of Corollary 4.3
nodes.statement:
As a direct consequence of \autoref{thm:partitive tree} and of \autoref{thm:transduce weakly-partitive tree},
we can produce, through a \CMSO[2]-transduction,
the partitive tree induced by a partitive set system
and naturally modeled by an $\{\mathsf{ancestor},\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace\}$-structure.
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of Theorem 4.2 and the absence of linear nodes in partitive trees.

nodes.name: CMSO[2]-transduction of partitive trees
nodes.statement:
There exists a non-deterministic \CMSO[2]-transduction~$\tau$
    such that,
    for each partitive set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
    represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure~$\mathbb{S}$
    and inducing the partitive tree $(T,\lambda)$
    represented as the $\{\mathsf{ancestor},\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$,
    we have~$\mathbb{T}\in\tau(\mathbb{S})$
    and every output in $\tau(\mathbb{S})$ is a partitive tree of $(U,\mathcal{S})$.
assumptions:
for each partitive set system~$(U,\mathcal{S})$
    represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{SET}}\xspace\}$-structure~$\mathbb{S}$
    and inducing the partitive tree $(T,\lambda)$
    represented as the $\{\mathsf{ancestor},\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{T}$
conclusions:
we have~$\mathbb{T}\in\tau(\mathbb{S})$
    and every output in $\tau(\mathbb{S})$ is a partitive tree of $(U,\mathcal{S})$.
nodes.label: cor:transduce partitive tree

nodes.name: Module of a graph
nodes.statement_short: A vertex set M such that every outside vertex is uniformly adjacent to (and from) all vertices of M.

nodes.name: Trivial modules
nodes.statement:
Clearly,
the empty set, $V(G)$, and all the singletons~$\{x\}$ for~$x\in V(G)$
are modules;
they are called \defd{the trivial modules} of~$G$.

nodes.name: Maximal module
nodes.statement:
We say a non-empty module~$M$ is \defd{maximal}
if it is not properly contained in any non-trivial module.

nodes.name: Full/empty adjacency between disjoint modules
nodes.statement:
Let~$M$ and~$M'$ be two disjoint non-empty modules of~$G$.
Considering the edges that go from~$M$ to~$M'$,
namely edges from the set $(M\times M')\cap E(G)$,
we have two possibilities:
either it is empty, or it is equal to~$M\times M'$.
We write~\defd{$\fullsucc[\not\to]{M}{M'}$} in the former case
and~\defd{$\fullsucc{M}{M'}$} in the latter.

nodes.name: Modular partition
nodes.statement:
A~\defd{modular partition} of~$G$
is a partition $\mathcal{P}=\{M_1,\ldots,M_\ell\}$ of~$V(G)$
such that every~$M_i$ is a non-empty module.

nodes.name: Maximal modular partition
nodes.statement:
A modular partition $\mathcal{P}=\{M_1,\dots,M_\ell\}$ is called \defd{maximal}
if it is non-trivial and every~$M_i$ is strong and maximal.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the maximal modular partition
nodes.statement: Note that every graph has exactly one maximal modular partition.
conclusions: every graph has exactly one maximal modular partition

nodes.name: Modular decomposition
nodes.statement:
A \defd{modular decomposition} of~$G$
is a rooted tree~$T$
in which the leaves are the vertices of~$G$,
and for each inner node~$t\in T$,
$t$ has at least two children
and the set~$L(T_t)$ is a module of~$G$.
differentia: the leaves are the vertices of~$G$
the set~$L(T_t)$ is a module of~$G$

nodes.name: Maximal modular decomposition
nodes.statement:
In a modular decomposition~$T$ of~$G$,
for each inner node~$t\in V(T)$
with children~$c_1,\ldots,c_r$,
the family $\mathcal{P}_t=\{L(T_{c_1}),\ldots,L(T_{c_r})\}$
is a modular partition of~$G[V(T_t)]$.
When each such partition is maximal,
the decomposition is unique
