nodes.statement_short: The enriched canonical split decomposition.

nodes.name: Three-stage composition
nodes.statement_short: Compose tau_1, tau_2, tau_3.

nodes.name: tau_1
nodes.statement: $\tau_1$: an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-interpretation which outputs the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{BIPART}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}$ from $\mathbb{G}$;
nodes.statement_short: MSO-interpretation adding splits.

nodes.name: tau_2
nodes.statement: $\tau_2$: the non-deterministic \CMSO[2]-transduction from \autoref{lem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-bipartitive family} which outputs the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{BIPART}}\xspace, \ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}\sqcup \mathbb{T}$ on input $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{S}$;
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.2 adds the laminar tree.

nodes.name: tau_3
nodes.statement:
$\tau_3$: an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-transduction which produces the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{c}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{H}$ from $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}\sqcup \mathbb{T}$.
    \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: MSO-transduction producing the decomposition.

nodes.name: Define tau_1
nodes.statement: To define $\tau_1$ it is sufficient to observe that there is an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula $\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{BIPART}}\xspace}(X,Y)$ with two monadic free-variables $X$ and $Y$ such that $\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{BIPART}}\xspace}$ is satisfied exactly when $\{X,Y\}$ is a split in $G$. As $\tau_2$ is constructed in \autoref{lem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-bipartitive family}, we are left with describing how to obtain $\tau_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Splits are MSO-definable; tau_2 comes from Lemma 5.2.

nodes.name: Represent markers
nodes.statement:
We first need to find unique representative for the vertices in $V(H)$. Recall that $V(H)$ consists of two marker vertices $v_X^Y$ and $v_Y^X$ for every strong bipartition $\{X,Y\}\in \ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}$.
    For ease of notation, we use the name $v^{V(G)\setminus\{u\}}_{\{u\}}$ for the leaf $u\in V(G)$ of $T$. Additionally, we
    set $v_s^t:=v_X^Y$ and $v_t^s:=v_Y^X$ where $\{s,t\}\in E(T)$ is the edge for which $L(T_s)=X$ and $L(T_t)=Y$ where $T_s$ is the component of $T-e$ containing $s$ and $T_t$ the component containing $t$. We use the following atomic transductions to ensure unique representatives for all vertices in $V(H)$. We first guess a colouring $R$ which identifies one non-leaf element of $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}\sqcup \mathbb{T}$ as root. We use this root element to interpret an auxiliary binary relation $\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace$ in the usual way. Now we copy the structure $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}\sqcup \mathbb{T}$ once introducing the binary relation $\copyV[1]$ in which $\copyV[1](x,y)$ indicates that $x$ is the copy of $y$. Assume that $\{s,t\}$ is an edge in $T$ corresponding to a strong bipartition in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(s,t)$ is satisfied. We use the original node $t$ to represent the marker $v_t^s$ and we use the copy of $t$ to represent the marker $v_s^t$. As every node has a unique parent in a rooted tree, for each marker the chosen representatives are unique. To express this we use the predicate $\ensuremath{\mathsf{marker}}\xspace(x,y,z)$ which expresses that $x$ is the representative of the marker $v_y^z$ defined as follows:
    $$\ensuremath{\mathsf{marker}}\xspace(x,y,z):= \Big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(z,y)\land x=y\Big)\lor \Big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{parent}}\xspace(y,z)\land \copyV[1](x,z)\Big).$$
nodes.statement_short: Guess a root, copy once, and represent each marker by a node or its copy via the marker predicate.

nodes.name: Filter to markers
nodes.statement: We now filter the universe only keeping all representatives of markers (recall that markers $v_{\{v\}}^{V(G)\setminus\{v\}}$ are the original vertices of $G$). We are left with defining the two edge relations $\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace$ and $\ensuremath{\mathsf{c}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace$. To do so, we use the previously defined functional predicate $\ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(t,s)$.
nodes.statement_short: Keep marker representatives; edge relations remain.

nodes.name: Define c-edges
nodes.statement:
First note that markers $v_t^s$ and $v_{t'}^{s'}$ are in the same component of $H$ if and only if\xspace $t=t'$. By \autoref{lem:edgesInSplitDecomposition} $v_t^sv_t^{s'}$ is an $\textsf{c}$-edge in $(H,F)$ if and only if\xspace there is an edge $uu'\in E(G)$ with $u\in L(T^t_s)$ and $u'\in L(T^t_{s'})$.
    Consequently, we can express $\ensuremath{\mathsf{c}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace$ as follows:
    \begin{align*}
        \phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{c}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace}(x,x'):=&\exists s \exists s' \exists t \exists y \exists y' \Big( \ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace(t,s)\land \ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace(t,s')\land \ensuremath{\mathsf{marker}}\xspace(x,t,s)\land
        \\*
        &\ensuremath{\mathsf{marker}}\xspace(x',t,s')\land
        y\in \ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(t,s)\land y'\in \ensuremath{\mathsf{leafset}}\xspace(t,s') \land E(y,y') \Big).
    \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 5.5, c-edges join markers of one node whose leaf sets are adjacent in G.

nodes.name: Define t-edges and output
nodes.statement:
On the other hand, the
    $\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace$-relation in $\mathbb{H}$ is the relation between pairs of markers and hence can be easily (re)-defined using the $\ensuremath{\mathsf{marker}}\xspace$ predicate by:
    $$\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace}(x,x'):=\exists y \exists z \big(\ensuremath{\mathsf{marker}}\xspace(x,y,z)\land \ensuremath{\mathsf{marker}}\xspace(x',z,y)\big).$$
    Finally, the transduction only keeps the relation $\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace$ and $\ensuremath{\mathsf{c}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace$.
nodes.statement_short: t-edges pair markers; keep only t-edge and c-edge.

nodes.name: Bi-join
nodes.statement:
A
\emph{bi-join} in an undirected graph $G$ is a bipartition $\{X,Y\}$ of $V(G)$ such that $\card{X}$, $\card{Y}\geq 1$ and there are subsets $X'\subseteq X$ and
$Y'\subseteq Y$ such that $X'\times Y'\cup (X\setminus X')\times (Y\setminus Y')\subseteq E(G)$, and there are no additional edges between $X$ and $Y$ in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: A bipartition {X,Y} whose cross edges are exactly X' x Y' together with (X\X') x (Y\Y') for some X', Y'.

nodes.name: Trivial bi-join and bi-join-prime graph
nodes.statement:
As for splits, a bi-join $\{X,Y\}$ is considered \emph{trivial} if $\card{X}=1$ or $\card{Y}=1$, and a graph is considered \emph{prime wrt bi-join} if it has only
trivial bi-joins.

nodes.name: Set of bi-joins of a graph
nodes.statement: Let us denote by $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G}$ the set of bi-joins of a graph $G$.

nodes.name: Bi-joins form a bipartitive family
nodes.statement: For every undirected graph $G$, the system $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G}$ is bipartitive.
assumptions: For every undirected graph $G$
conclusions: the system $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G}$ is bipartitive.

nodes.name: CMSO[2]-transduction of the laminar tree of strong bi-joins
nodes.statement:
A corollary of \autoref{thm:join-bipartitive} and \autoref{lem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-bipartitive family} we get the existence of a \CMSO[2]-transduction taking as input an
undirected graph $G$ represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}$ and outputting the laminar tree representing the set of strong bi-joins of
$G$.
assumptions: undirected graph $G$ represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}$
conclusions: the existence of a \CMSO[2]-transduction

nodes.name: Neighbourhood equivalence relative to X
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a subset of $V(G)$, let $\equiv_X$ be the relation on $X\times X$ where $x\equiv_X y$ if $N(x)\cap V(G)\setminus X = N(y)\cap V(G)\setminus X$.

nodes.name: Equivalence classes u_1, u_2 of a node
nodes.statement:
Let $T$ be the bipartitive tree of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G}$, and for a node $u$, let $u_1$ and $u_2$ be the, at most two, equivalence classes of
$\equiv_{L(T_u)}$.

nodes.name: Node graph G_u
nodes.statement:
For every node $u$ of $T$, let's denote by $G_u$ the graph whose vertex set is $\{v_1,v_2\mid v$ is a neighbor of $u\}$, and there is an edge
$z_iz_j$ in $G_u$ if there is $x\in z_i$ and $y\in z_j$ such that $xy\in E(G)$.

nodes.name: Skeleton graph
nodes.statement:
The \emph{skeleton graph} associated with $T$ is the graph obtained by taking
first the disjoint union of the graphs $G_u$, for all nodes $u$ of $T$, and then adding $\textsf{t}$-edges between copies of same equivalence classes.
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint union of the node graphs G_u, with t-edges joining copies of the same equivalence class.

nodes.name: Properties of the skeleton graph
nodes.statement_short: Adjacency in G is alternating-path connectivity in the skeleton graph, and contracting the G_u recovers the bipartitive tree.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a connected graph and let $H$ be its skeleton graph.
conclusions: two vertices $x$ and $y$ of $G$ are adjacent if and only if there is an alternating path between $x$ and $y$ in $H$;

nodes.name: CMSO[2]-transduction of the skeleton graph
nodes.statement:
There exists a non-deterministic \CMSO[2]-transduction $\tau$
    such that for any connected graph $G$ represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}$,
    $\tau(\mathbb{G})$ is non-empty
    and every output in~$\tau(\mathbb{G})$
    is equal to some $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{c}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{H}$ representing the skeleton graph of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-deterministic CMSO[2]-transduction outputs the skeleton graph (bi-join decomposition) of any connected graph.
assumptions: for any connected graph $G$ represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}$
conclusions:
$\tau(\mathbb{G})$ is non-empty
    and every output in~$\tau(\mathbb{G})$
    is equal to some
nodes.label: thm:bi-join1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.7
nodes.statement:
Let $G$ be a connected graph represented by the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}$, $(V(G), \ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G})$ the bipartitive set system consisting of all bi-joins
    of $G$ represented by the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{BIPART}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{B}$, $H$ its skeleton graph represented by the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{c}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{H}$ and $T$ represented by the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace\}$-structure, the bipartitive tree of $(V(G),\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G})$.

    Our first step is to transduce $\mathbb{B}$ from $\mathbb{G}$. For this it is sufficient to observe that we can easily define an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula $\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{BIPART}}\xspace}(X,Y)$ with two monadic free-variables $X$ and $Y$ which defines bi-joins $\{X,Y\}$ of $G$.

    Since $\mathbb{B}$ is bipartitive we can apply \autoref{lem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-bipartitive family} to transduce $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}\sqcup \mathbb{T}$ from $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}$. In the following we describe how to transduce $\mathbb{H}$ from $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}\sqcup \mathbb{T}$.

    Contrary to the case of the canonical split decomposition, we cannot deterministically deduce, from $T$, the four markers associated with the bi-join displayed by
    $T$. However, since the set $\{L(T_u)\mid u$ is a node of $T\}$ is a laminar set system, one can use \autoref{cor:4 bi-colouring} to
    non-deterministically associate with each node $u$ of $T$ a leaf as done in the proof of \autoref{thm:transduce laminar tree}. For each node $u$, let's denote
    by $u_1$ this representative. Knowing $u_1$ and $u$, one can make a copy of $u$ and relate it to the equivalence of $\equiv_{L(T_u)}$ not containing
    $u_1$. Now that we can create copies, for each node $u$, representing the two equivalence classes of $\equiv_u$, we leave, to the reader, the description of the
    transduction outputting the desired skeleton graph, as one can use the same copying technique as the one in \autoref{thm:split}.
nodes.statement_short: Define bi-joins in MSO, transduce their tree (Lemma 5.2), and use the four bi-colourings of Corollary 3.10 to pick representatives distinguishing the two equivalence classes per node.

nodes.name: Setup and define bi-joins
nodes.statement:
Let $G$ be a connected graph represented by the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}$, $(V(G), \ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G})$ the bipartitive set system consisting of all bi-joins
    of $G$ represented by the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{BIPART}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{B}$, $H$ its skeleton graph represented by the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{c}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{H}$ and $T$ represented by the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{degenerate}}\xspace\}$-structure, the bipartitive tree of $(V(G),\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G})$.

    Our first step is to transduce $\mathbb{B}$ from $\mathbb{G}$. For this it is sufficient to observe that we can easily define an \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace-formula $\phi_{\ensuremath{\mathsf{BIPART}}\xspace}(X,Y)$ with two monadic free-variables $X$ and $Y$ which defines bi-joins $\{X,Y\}$ of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the bi-join system, skeleton graph and tree; bi-joins are MSO-definable.

nodes.name: Tree via Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement: Since $\mathbb{B}$ is bipartitive we can apply \autoref{lem:transduce laminar tree induced by weakly-bipartitive family} to transduce $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}\sqcup \mathbb{T}$ from $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}$. In the following we describe how to transduce $\mathbb{H}$ from $\mathbb{G}\sqcup \mathbb{B}\sqcup \mathbb{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.2 adds the bipartitive tree.

nodes.name: Representatives via bi-colourings
nodes.statement:
Contrary to the case of the canonical split decomposition, we cannot deterministically deduce, from $T$, the four markers associated with the bi-join displayed by
    $T$. However, since the set $\{L(T_u)\mid u$ is a node of $T\}$ is a laminar set system, one can use \autoref{cor:4 bi-colouring} to
    non-deterministically associate with each node $u$ of $T$ a leaf as done in the proof of \autoref{thm:transduce laminar tree}. For each node $u$, let's denote
    by $u_1$ this representative. Knowing $u_1$ and $u$, one can make a copy of $u$ and relate it to the equivalence of $\equiv_{L(T_u)}$ not containing
    $u_1$. Now that we can create copies, for each node $u$, representing the two equivalence classes of $\equiv_u$, we leave, to the reader, the description of the
    transduction outputting the desired skeleton graph, as one can use the same copying technique as the one in \autoref{thm:split}.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 3.10 picks a leaf per node to separate the two equivalence classes; finish as for splits.

nodes.name: Characteristic graph
nodes.statement:
For a node $u$ and $x_1,\ldots, x_p$ leaves in the connected components of $T\setminus u$, not two of them in the same connected component, let
$G[x_1,\ldots, x_p]$ be the \emph{characteristic graph} associated with $u$ and $\{x_1,\ldots, x_p\}$.

nodes.name: Characteristic graphs detect degenerate nodes
nodes.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph and let $T$ be the partitive tree of
  $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G}$. For every node $u$ of $T$ and every characteristic graph $G_u$ of $u$, $G_u$ is degenerate if and only if $u$ is degenerate.
assumptions:
Let $G$ be a graph and let $T$ be the partitive tree of
  $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G}$.
conclusions: $G_u$ is degenerate if and only if $u$ is degenerate.

nodes.name: Seidel switch
nodes.statement:
For a graph $H$ and $W$ a subset of $V(H)$, the
\emph{Seidel switch of $H$ at $W$}, denoted by $\overline{H}^W$, is the graph with $V(H)$ as vertex set and edge set
$E(H[W])\cup E(H\setminus W) \cup \{xy\mid x\in W, y\notin W$ and $xy\notin E(H)\}$ \cite{seidel1991}.

nodes.name: Composition of Seidel switches
nodes.statement:
One checks that if $H'$ is obtained by a Seidel switch on
$W'$ in $\overline{H}^W$, then $H'=\overline{H}^{W\bigtriangleup W'}$ (see for instance \cite[Lemma 11.1]{ehrenfeuchtHR1999}).
assumptions:
$H'$ is obtained by a Seidel switch on
$W'$ in $\overline{H}^W$
conclusions: $H'=\overline{H}^{W\bigtriangleup W'}$

nodes.name: Seidel equivalence
nodes.statement:
Now, two graphs $H$ and $H'$ are \emph{Seidel equivalent} if one is isomorphic to a Seidel switch
of the other.

nodes.name: Bi-joins are invariant under Seidel switch
nodes.statement:
Let $H$ be a graph and let $W$ be a subset of $V(H)$. Then, $\{X,Y\}$ is a bi-join in $H$ if and only if $\{X,Y\}$ is a
  bi-join of $\overline{H}^W$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be a graph and let $W$ be a subset of $V(H)$.
conclusions:
$\{X,Y\}$ is a bi-join in $H$ if and only if $\{X,Y\}$ is a
  bi-join of $\overline{H}^W$.

nodes.name: Seidel classes correspond to two-graphs
nodes.statement: It has been proved that Seidel equivalence classes are in bijection with the set of \emph{two-graphs} \cite{seidel1991}.
conclusions: Seidel equivalence classes are in bijection with the set of \emph{two-graphs}

nodes.name: Two-graph
nodes.statement:
A \emph{two-graph} is a pair
$(V,\Omega)$ where
 $\Omega$ is a family of subsets of size $3$ on the finite set $V$ such that each subset of size $4$ of $V$ contains an even number of subsets in $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Two-graph of a graph
nodes.statement:
For
 every undirected graph $H$, one can associate a two-graph $\Omega(H)$ where $\{x,y,z\}$ belongs to $\Omega(H)$ if $x,y$ and $z$ are all pairwise distinct and
 the number of edges in $H[\{x,y,z\}]$ is odd.

nodes.name: Graph of a two-graph at x
nodes.statement:
Conversely, if $(V,\Omega)$ is a two-graph and $x$ is in $V$, then one can construct a graph $H(\Omega,x)$ with vertex set $V$ and edge
 set $\{yz\mid \{x,y,z\}\in \Omega\}$.

nodes.name: Two-graphs and Seidel equivalence
assumptions: Let $V$ be a finite set of size at least $3$.
conclusions: for every two-graph $(V,\Delta)$, the graph $H(\Delta,x)$ is such that $\Omega(H(\Delta,x))=(V,\Delta)$;
two graphs $G$ and $H$ with vertex set $V$ are Seidel equivalent if and only if $\Omega(G)=\Omega(H)$.

nodes.name: Join of two-graphs
nodes.statement:
For two two-graphs $(V_1,\Omega_1)$ and $(V_2,\Omega_2)$ and $v_1 \in V_1$ and $v_2\in V_2$, their \emph{join wrt $v_1$ and $v_2$} is the two-graph $(V_1\cup V_2\setminus
 \{v_1,v_2\},\Omega)$ where $\Omega = \{\{x,y,z\} \subseteq V_1\cup V_2\setminus
 \{v_1,v_2\}\mid \{x,y,z\}\in \Omega_1 \cup \Omega_2$ or $\{x,y,v_1\}\in \Omega_1, \{z,t,v_2\}\in \Omega_2$ for some $t$, or $\{x,y,v_2\}\in \Omega_2, \{z,t,v_1\}\in \Omega_1$ for some $t\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Glue two two-graphs at marker elements v_1, v_2, keeping old triples and adding mixed triples through the markers.

nodes.name: Two-graph of a graph decomposes along a bi-join
nodes.statement:
A corollary of \autoref{thm:seidel-equiv} is that if $\{X,Y\}$ is a bi-join of a graph $H$ with
 $X\times Y\cap E(H) = X'\times Y' \cup (X\setminus X')\times (Y\setminus Y')$, if we let $H[X]$ (resp. $H[Y]$) as defined for split decomposition with the
 marker $v_X^Y$ (resp. $v_Y^X$) adjacent to $X'$ (resp. $Y'$), $\Omega(H)$ is equal to the join of $\Omega(H[X])$ and of $\Omega(H[Y])$ wrt $v_X^Y$ and
 $v_Y^X$.
assumptions:
$\{X,Y\}$ is a bi-join of a graph $H$ with
 $X\times Y\cap E(H) = X'\times Y' \cup (X\setminus X')\times (Y\setminus Y')$
conclusions:
$\Omega(H)$ is equal to the join of $\Omega(H[X])$ and of $\Omega(H[Y])$ wrt $v_X^Y$ and
 $v_Y^X$

nodes.name: Complementing marker adjacency preserves the two-graph
nodes.statement: As observed in \cite{raoThesis}, making $v_X^Y$ (resp. $v_Y^X$) adjacent to $X\setminus X'$ (resp. $Y\setminus Y'$) gives the same two-graph.
conclusions: gives the same two-graph

nodes.name: Seidel skeleton
nodes.statement:
As a corollary, if we associate with each node $u$ of the bipartitive tree $T$ of $G$ any characteristic graph and join all of them using $\textsf{t}$-edges as in the
split decomposition, one obtains a structure, called \emph{Seidel skeleton}, representing the Seidel equivalence class of $G$, which can by definition transduces $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Join arbitrary characteristic graphs of all tree nodes via t-edges as in split decomposition; it represents G's Seidel class.

nodes.name: Seidel skeleton defines a Seidel-equivalent graph
nodes.statement:
Let $T$ be the bipartive tree of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G}$ and let $S(G,T)$ be the Seidel skeleton of $T$. If $S(G,T)$ is considered as
  a split decomposition and $H$ is the graph it defines, then $G$ is Seidel equivalent to $H$.
assumptions: Let $T$ be the bipartive tree of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}_\mathsf{join}^G}$ and let $S(G,T)$ be the Seidel skeleton of $T$.

$S(G,T)$ is considered as
  a split decomposition and $H$ is the graph it defines
conclusions: $G$ is Seidel equivalent to $H$.
nodes.label: lem:seidel-equiv2

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 5.9
nodes.statement: A direct corollary is the desired transduction.
nodes.statement_short: Direct corollary of Lemma 5.8 combined with the split-decomposition transduction technique.

nodes.name: CMSO[2]-transduction of the Seidel skeleton
nodes.statement:
There exists a non-deterministic \CMSO[2]-transduction $\tau$
    such that for any connected graph $G$ represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}$,
    $\tau(\mathbb{G})$ is non-empty
    and every output in~$\tau(\mathbb{G})$ is equal to some $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{t}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathsf{c}\text-\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{H}$ representing the Seidel skeleton of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-deterministic CMSO[2]-transduction outputs a Seidel skeleton (bi-join decomposition of the Seidel class) of any connected graph.
assumptions: for any connected graph $G$ represented as the $\{\ensuremath{\mathsf{edge}}\xspace\}$-structure $\mathbb{G}$
conclusions:
$\tau(\mathbb{G})$ is non-empty
    and every output in~$\tau(\mathbb{G})$ is equal to some
nodes.label: thm:bi-join2

nodes.name: Further applications of the weakly-bipartitive transduction
nodes.statement:
It is worth
mentioning that \autoref{thm:transduce weakly-bipartitive tree} can be also used to \CMSO-transduce canonical decompositions of other structures such as Tutte's
decomposition of matroids or generally 
split-decompositions of submodular functions \cite{cunningham1982decomposition} or modular decompositions of $2$-structures \cite{ehrenfeuchtHR1999} or of hypergraphs
\cite{HabibMMZ22}.

nodes.name: Is counting necessary to transduce these decompositions?
nodes.statement:
Also, naturally, the
question arises whether counting is necessary or whether \ensuremath{\operatorname{MSO}}\xspace is sufficient to transduce such decompositions.

nodes.name: CMSO-transducing rank-decompositions via split decomposition
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a class of graphs for which there is, for every $k$, a \CMSO-transduction $\varphi_{\mathcal{C},k}$, that takes as input a
  graph $G$ in $\mathcal{C}$ and outputs a rank-decomposition of $G$ of width at most $f(k)$, for some computable function $f$. Then, for every positive integer
  $k$ and for every class of graphs
  $\mathcal{D}$ whose prime graphs with respect to split-decomposition belong to $\mathcal{C}$, there is a \CMSO-transduction
  $\psi_{\mathcal{D},k}$ that takes as input a graph $G$ in $\mathcal{D}$ and outputs a rank-decomposition of $G$ of width at most $f(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: If rank-decompositions of bounded width are CMSO-transducible on a class C, they are also on every class whose split-prime graphs lie in C.
assumptions:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a class of graphs for which there is, for every $k$, a \CMSO-transduction $\varphi_{\mathcal{C},k}$, that takes as input a
  graph $G$ in $\mathcal{C}$ and outputs a rank-decomposition of $G$ of width at most $f(k)$, for some computable function $f$.
conclusions:
there is a \CMSO-transduction
  $\psi_{\mathcal{D},k}$ that takes as input a graph $G$ in $\mathcal{D}$ and outputs a rank-decomposition of $G$ of width at most $f(k)$.
nodes.label: thm:cor-cmso-rank-dec

nodes.name: CMSO-transducing rank-decompositions for bounded prime graphs
nodes.statement:
A corollary of \autoref{thm:cor-cmso-rank-dec} is that, for any fixed
$k$, there is a \CMSO-transduction that computes a rank-decomposition of small width for any graph belonging to a graph class whose prime graphs have sizes
bounded by $k$ or prime graphs have linear rank-width bounded by $k$.
assumptions:
for any fixed
$k$
conclusions:
there is a \CMSO-transduction that computes a rank-decomposition of small width for any graph belonging to a graph class whose prime graphs have sizes
bounded by $k$ or prime graphs have linear rank-width bounded by $k$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a family of bipartitions of a set $U$ and $a\in U$ any element.
    First observe that $(U,\mathcal{S}_a)$ is a set system
    as $\emptyset\notin \mathcal{S}_a$ (since $\{\emptyset,U\}\notin \mathcal{B}$),
    $U\in \mathcal{S}_a$,
    and $\{b\}\in \mathcal{S}_a$ for every $b\in U$ (since~$\{a\}\in\mathcal{S}_a$ and for~$b\neq a$, $\{\{b\},U\setminus \{b\}\}\in \mathcal{B}$).

    To argue the second assertion, assume that $T$ is the laminar tree of the set system $(U,\mathcal{S}_a)$. First observe that in the set system $(U,\mathcal{S}_a)$ the element $a$ is not contained in any set apart from $U$ and $\{a\}$ and hence the leaf $\{a\}$ is a child of the root $U$ of $T$. Additionally, the set $U\setminus \{a\}$ is in $S_a$ as the bipartition $(\{a\},U\setminus \{a\})$ is in $\mathcal{B}$ by definition and hence $U\setminus \{a\}$ is also a child of the root $U$ of $T$. Let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by removing node $U$, making all edges undirected and adding an edge from node $\{a\}$ to node $U\setminus \{a\}$. Indeed, by our previous observations, $T'$ is an undirected tree. Furthermore, there is a correspondence between elements of $U$ and the leaves of $T'$ (element $b\in U$ corresponds to leaf $\{b\}$ of $T'$). To check that $T'$ is indeed the laminar tree of $T$, we need to verify that for each bipartition $\{X,Y\}$ in $\mathcal{B}$ there is exactly one edge $e$ of $T'$ such that $X=L(T'_1)$ and $Y=L(T'_2)$ for the two connected components $T'_1,T'_2$ of $T'-e$. We say that the edge \emph{$e$ implements the bipartition $\{X,Y\}$}.
    Assume that $\{X,Y\}$ is any bipartition from $\mathcal{B}$. First consider the case that $\{X,Y\}$ is the bipartition $\{\{a\},U\setminus\{a\}\}$. Then $\{X,Y\}$ is clearly implemented by the edge $\{\{a\},U\setminus\{a\}\}$ of $T'$. Now assume that $\{X,Y\}$ is any other bipartition in $\mathcal{B}$ and assume, without loss of generality, that $a\in Y$. Hence, $X\in \mathcal{S}_a$. Let $X'$ be the parent of $X$ in $T$. Note that $X$ must be a proper subset of $U\setminus \{a\}$ as by our assumption $\{X,Y\}$ is not the partition $\{\{a\},U\setminus \{a\}$ and hence $X'$ cannot be $U$. As we only deleted edge incident to $U$ in our construction of $T'$, $\{X,X'\}$ is an edge in $T'$ which clearly implements the bipartition $\{X,Y\}$. Finally, every bipartition $\{X,Y\}\in \mathcal{B}$ is clearly implemented by only one edge as every inner node of the tree $T'$ has degree at least three. Therefore, $T'$ is the laminar tree of $(U,\mathcal{B})$.
